subsubtopic: MISSISSAUGA DISASTER-TRANSPORTATION OF HAZARDOUS PRODUCTS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at 11.45 Saturday evening, November 10, 1979, a CP train derailed. This train was carrying a number of jumbo cars containing propane, butane, caustic soda, other petrochemicals and, most dangerous of all, chlorine.
As a result of the derailment, there were a number of explosions and severe fires, and these fires are still burning at the present time. The Peel regional police force and the Ontario provincial police, assisted by police officers from metropolitan Toronto and other neighbouring municipalities, together with the Red Cross and other emergency measures' people, including the Mississauga fire department, took command of the situation. Because of the danger of leakage of chlorine gas and the possible rupture of the chlorine tanker, all of the citizens from my riding and the neighbouring ridings of Mississauga North, to a large extent Oakville and Etobicoke-Lakeshore, were evacuated in a peaceful and well organized fashion.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, since this emergency has been handled with such dispatch and confidence, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Mississauga North (Mr. Jupp) and the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis):
That this House does extend its commendation to all those directly involved in attending to the emergency arising from a CP Rail train derailment at Mississauga, Ontario, particularly since as a result of their actions, there has been to date no loss of life, and that this House does direct the Minister of Transport to assure this House and the people of Canada that a full and impartial investigation will be held concerning this accident and concerning the transportation of dangerous goods.

In view of the fact that budget cuts have greatly reduced the supply and development of new postal services in Canada, which has resulted in serious deficiencies in the services pro-

subsubtopic: MISSISSAUGA DISASTER-TRANSPORTATION OF HAZARDOUS PRODUCTS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the emergency created by the derailment of a train in Mississauga, Ontario, carrying propane, chlorine and other dangerous substances, in view of the fact that over 200,000 people have had to be evacuated from their homes, and in view of the continuing danger posed by this accident to the health and safety of tens of thousands of citizens in the Toronto area, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie):
That this House calls upon the government to launch an immediate investigation into the causes and consequences of this derailment and to introduce immediately legislation concerning the transportation of dangerous goods which would provide for full and complete labelling of the dangerous substances, a program of special safety and precautionary measures and provision for the protection of the population from the transportation of these substances.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have a question for the Minister of Transport of which I have given him notice. In view of the disastrous derailment which occurred in Mississauga this past weekend, in this instance can the minister advise the House what additional precautionary methods were taken in view of the fact the railroad was transporting combustible products and poisonous gases.

speechtext:
In
response to the hon. member's question, Mr. Speaker, I think he and other hon. members know that the Canadian Transport Commission has announced that a formal public inquiry will be held to investigate all matters concerning this unfortunate incident. I think we shall have to await the outcome of that inquiry to determine whether or not all rules and regulations were complied with in relation to this unfortunate incident.

speechtext:
I am not concerned about what happened after the fact; 1 am concerned about what happened before the fact.
I should like to know from the minister what his officials have advised him with respect to additional precautionary measures taken in all cases where transportation of hazardous products takes place.

subsubtopic: MISSISSAUGA DISASTER-TRANSPORTATION OF HAZARDOUS PRODUCTS-SAFETY PRECAUTIONS
speechtext:
As the hon. member knows, responsibility for the surveillance of safety with respect to railways lies with the Canadian Transport Commission. Following their announcement of the inquiry, 1 have asked the CTC to focus particularly on the question of adequate safety standards, the ensurance of an appropriate level of maintenance and the adequacy of the inspection system: the suggestion was made in committee that the number of inspectors was insufficient. Evidence of this was adduced in the committee and provided by the president of the CTC.
1 might say, as well, that we are in a position to introduce legislation with respect to the transportation of dangerous goods. This was announced in the House by the President of the Privy Council on October 11,1 believe. The bill is in the final stages of preparation and could be introduced within the next week or ten days.

I am in a position, now, to state to the House that there has been general agreement on all elements of that piece of legislation; it is in its final drafting stages. I am pleased the hon. member wants this legislation brought forward, and 1 hope he will be disposed to deal with it in expeditious fashion when it is introduced.

circumstances having regard to that formula, the government would be very pleased to act.

subsubtopic: MISSISSAUGA DISASTER-TRANSPORTATION OF HAZARDOUS PRODUCTS-INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, have a question for the Minister of Transport arising from the serious threat to human life and health caused by the CPR wreck in Mississauga. One month ago today I was assured in this House by the Minister of the Environment that a bill concerning the transportation of dangerous goods would be introduced, and I quote, "soon". Not soon enough, it appears.
Is the Minister of Transport aware that on Thursday of last week the chairman of the Canadian Transport Commission indicated to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications that the CTC budget was insufficient? It was not a question of maybe there were not enough rail inspectors; there were not enough inspectors for the proper carrying out of the CTC's responsibility for rail safety in Canada. In the words of the commissioner himself, there are only some 78 rail inspectors, when there should be 178.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MISSISSAUGA DISASTER-TRANSPORTATION OF HAZARDOUS PRODUCTS-INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext: Order, please. Would the hon. member put his question.

subsubtopic: MISSISSAUGA DISASTER-TRANSPORTATION OF HAZARDOUS PRODUCTS-INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext: Is the minister aware of that?

subsubtopic: MISSISSAUGA DISASTER-TRANSPORTATION OF HAZARDOUS PRODUCTS-INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am aware of the evidence which was presented to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. As a result of this incident and the inquiry which has been ordered by the CTC, and as 1 indicated to the hon. member for Stormont-Dundas, 1 have asked the CTC to pay particular attention to the adequacy of safety standards, the level of safety standards, the adequacy of maintenance standards and frequency of maintenance, as well as the adequacy in the number of inspectors to carry out this job. That is certainly part and parcel of this inquiry. We will await the outcome of the inquiry and the government will act on the basis of the forthcoming recommendations.

subsubtopic: MISSISSAUGA DISASTER-TRANSPORTATION OF HAZARDOUS PRODUCTS-INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hopefully the minister will indicate to the President of the Treasury Board that restraint ought to be lifted in this vital area. My second question is with regard to the fact that restraint with regard to rail safety is not the sole prerogative of government. Is the minister aware of the cutbacks in the area of rail safety initiated by the railroads themselves?
Will the minister tell the House what his department is doing about this in the ordinary course of its responsibilities, and has the minister indicated to the railroads the unacceptability of these cutbacks which have taken place, for instance, in the area of track and car inspection and maintenance?
November 12, 1979

subsubtopic: MISSISSAUGA DISASTER-TRANSPORTATION OF HAZARDOUS PRODUCTS-INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it would be in the interests of this House and all hon. members to await the outcome of this inquiry, to establish whether there have been sufficient levels of safety and whether we have had adequate numbers of people engaged in safety surveillance. Simply because we have had an incident does not necessarily mean that the whole system has broken down. There has been an indication by the committee; we are acting on its recommendations and will continue to act pending the recommendations which will flow from the inquiry which will be undertaken very soon.

subsubtopic: MISSISSAUGA DISASTER-TRANSPORTATION OF HAZARDOUS PRODUCTS-INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, is the minister saying that in the absence of the event in Mississauga this past weekend, nothing would have happened in the Department of Transport with regard to these things?

subsubtopic: MISSISSAUGA DISASTER-TRANSPORTATION OF HAZARDOUS PRODUCTS-INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MISSISSAUGA DISASTER-TRANSPORTATION OF HAZARDOUS PRODUCTS-INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext: My final question, Mr. Speaker, and it is a very serious question, is: Will the minister consider broadening the emphasis of the suggested legislation in this area to include provision in the transport of dangerous goods legislation for the eventual rerouting of dangerous goods around residential areas, where that is possible, so that we do not have to face the kind of risk the people of Mississauga faced this past weekend?

subsubtopic: MISSISSAUGA DISASTER-TRANSPORTATION OF HAZARDOUS PRODUCTS-INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am glad the hon. member says he is going to be serious. 1 am not sure whether his suggestion is serious. 1 am sure this is a matter which naturally will be dealt with by the inquiry.
In so far as the government's position with respect to the transportation of dangerous goods is concerned, I indicated earlier that the legislation is in its final drafting stage. It will probably be introduced within the next week or ten days. Because of the complexity of the application of laws with respect to the movement of dangerous goods, this legislation will require the co-operation and concurrence of provinces, municipalities and the industry. We have undertaken to ensure that this bill will not only be supported by but also abided with by all components of the industry.
When the bill comes in, I can assure the hon. member that it will be acceptable to the provinces and to the industry. We hope the hon. member will support the legislation and co-operate so that it can be passed in an expeditious fashion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I very much thank the hon. member for giving me notice of this question. subsubtopic: MR. GAMBLE - RECOGNITION OF MEMBERS DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege arises out of the practice which has been established and acknowledged by yourself in recognizing speakers in the House during question period, and also the practice that has developed in allowing supplementaries.
It is my view that compliance with Standing Order 5 for all members to attend the service of the House is surely not
Privilege-Mr. Gamble
sufficient. In order to discharge their duties, members of the House must not only be seen but also be heard.
On Thursday last the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) on two separate occasions when commenting upon an approval which had emanated from this side of the House of some comments he had made used the expression "backbencher" in designating certain members of the House, myself included, since I was involved in the commendation of some of his remarks.
I believe that designation carried with it a concept of a lesser or a greater degree of right to participate in proceedings. In the month that 1 have sat in this House I have recognized that there is most certainly a distinction between those who sit in the front benches and are recognized during question period and those who sit in the rear benches and stand without recognition. 1 consider that it is absolutely vital for all members in discharging their obligations in this House to be dealt with in a similar manner.
My comments most assuredly are not directed at Your Honour in the exercise of your judgment. I realize that this issue comes close to the issue of the order of the House. However, it is fundamental to my rights as a member in discharging my obligations to my constituents and to breaking down any distinction between those members of this House who may be first class and recognized speedily and those who may be second class and may or may not be recognized at all or at some future or remote time. That is why I draw this matter to the attention of this House.
It cannot be reasonably suggested that because I happen to sit as a member of the government the questions I intend to pose are cream-puff ones for ministers of the Crown. I submit that I am entitled to pose those questions which 1 believe are urgent, to the same extent as members who pose questions from the other side of the House.
I would urgently request that the issue of recognition be a matter to be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections for determination.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. GAMBLE - RECOGNITION OF MEMBERS DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
Of course, 1 cannot let this go further. The hon. member gave me notice that he would raise a question of privilege. He will realize at once that he has no question of privilege, and I cannot hear further contributions to a nonquestion of privilege.
The hon. member will have to realize that the discretion of the Chair is entire in the matter of recognition of members. There is, of course, a fundamental difference, not so much in rank or importance, because all members have equal importance, but in the nature of members who support the government and members who are in opposition to the government when it comes to the functioning of question period. There is a completely different process involved, one of a very fundamental nature, when those who are putting questions are in opposition to the government compared with when those same questions are put by members in support of the government. That has long been recognized, not only by this Parliament but by every Parliament, in terms of their fundamental difference. To suggest that the time during question period ought in any

November 12, 1979
Privilege-Mr. Gamble
way to be equally divided among all members of the House- except those in cabinet who are therefore charged with the responsibility of answering the questions-is a suggestion that is not in keeping with the fundamental difference between those in opposition and those in government.
I have recognized as a matter of principle from the very first day that government members equally have a right to ask questions. However, I have never granted supplementaries to government members because to grant a supplementary is, in my opinion, to recognize that the question contains in it an attack on a minister that has not been completed and that deserves further clarification. It is fundamentally erroneous to suggest that government members in putting questions are attacking in the same way as opposition members. There is a difference of very fundamental nature.
The hon. member put a question today which I think the member and the minister involved will agree, as he says, was certainly not handed to the minister as any "cream puff', to use his description. That, if he will examine the record, is the exception rather than the rule in our experience in the last four weeks, and not only in the last four weeks but during the last five years. There is no fundamental change between one Parliament and another.
I have from the very first day always recognized a government questioner during question period as an acceptance of that right, which lies with members like himself as of right, to participate in the question period. Today when the proportion of opposition members ready to ask questions was not as high as it has been on other days, I recognized three members from the government side, which is a recognition that in certain circumstances the proportion from the hon. member's side of the House can be increased. His question was one of them, because he tried two or three days ago.
I hope the hon. member will realize he prevailed over some of his colleagues today because a couple of days ago he was trying to get recognized and failed. That is precisely the same criteria applied to the other side of the House. Members who got up today were those who have been trying for a day or two without success and therefore ought to be favoured today. I follow the same practice for both sides of the House.
The hon. member will also realize there are very severe limitations on all of us in this exercise and we have to do the best we can with the time available.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF VIEW ON BREACH OF LAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members on both sides of the House who strove to make my position clear for me on this very important issue. I want to say that my view with regard to the question of breach of law is very simple, that no person be he ever so great shall be above

the law. I am glad that the Solicitor General (Mr. Lawrence) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) seem to agree with that.
I would vigorously oppose any attempt to change that particular rule. It is a position I took some years ago when the then prime minister and members of his cabinet were in breach of the law in that they broke the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act. I took very strong measures to try and have them impeached at that time. Unfortunately I was unsuccessful. That was a previous Speaker. Who knows, Your Honour may have different ideas about impeachment.

subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-S.O. 43 MOTIONS-RECOGNITION OF MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order concerning Standing Order 43 and ask for clarification from the Chair with regard to a certain aspect of that Standing Order.
I have always assumed, rightly or wrongly, and I assume many other members have as well, that Standing Order 43 existed for the purpose of enabling any member, regardless whether he was in government, official opposition or whatever party, to raise a matter of urgent and pressing necessity either pertaining to his constituency or to the country as a whole, and that therefore as many people in the government as in the official opposition, the NDP and so on could be recognized. I raise this point to gain clarification from the Chair as to whether there is a quota system of any kind with regard to the right of any member to raise a matter that concerns him and which he feels is of urgent necessity.
Today there were only two members in the House from the Social Credit group and they were recognized for a motion under Standing Order 43. There are over 130 on the government side.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-S.O. 43 MOTIONS-RECOGNITION OF MEMBERS
speechtext:
The hon. member raises a point I am sure the House will want to hear about. The matter of Standing Order 43 poses to a certain extent a problem similar to the one just raised by the hon. member for York North (Mr. Gamble) concerning questions, although not to the same extent. Therefore, I would perhaps not be as strict in trying to maintain a different ratio with the members on Standing Order 43 motions that I would with questions.
November 12, 1979

Today the hon. member's colleague was given the floor first over any other member of the House in order to move his rather important motion related to the recent train derailment. He was, and I think the record might clarify this, given a pretty generous share of the time allotted to Standing Order 43. In turn, because the motion carried, it took a bit more time, all of which was quite appropriate.
It would therefore not be my tendency to go back to the same side of the floor the second time until I assured pretty generous treatment to the opposite side. That was the factor that influenced me today. Had it been another kind of day in which perhaps the hon. member's colleague had put a more routine question which was set aside by the House and not received, the likelihood of two or perhaps even three members from that side being recognized for applications under Standing Order 43 would not be out of the way. I do not say that is assured, but it is more likely.
The fact that it was put today had more to do with the single motion in which preferential treatment was quite properly given to the hon. member's colleague from Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) with respect to the very urgent and serious matter that happened there rather than to any long standing policy to receive perhaps only one such application from the government side on any given day.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN COMPANIES-DEDUCTION OF CAPITAL LOSSES
speechtext:
1.	Does the government intend to discontinue allowable taxable capital losses on Canadian companies?
2.	Will such losses continue to be deductible for foreign holdings?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ron Ritchie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: CANADIAN COMPANIES-DEDUCTION OF CAPITAL LOSSES
speechtext:
1.	One of the objectives of the tax system is to encourage equity investments by Canadians in Canadian companies. In this context, a review is underway of possible measures that would make such investments more attractive to more Canadians. The treatment of capital losses is an integral part of our capital gains system and the discontinuance of a deduction for allowable capital losses would reduce rather than enhance the attractiveness of investments in Canadian companies. Accordingly, so long as gains are taxable, losses should remain deductible.
2.	The recognition of capital gains and losses on foreign property is an integral part of the capital gains tax system.
Since the gains on foreign property are taxable, it would be inequitable to deny the deduction for losses. There is no intention to restrict the existing deduction of capital losses on any property from the gain on any other property, domestic or foreign.

subtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACTS, 1867 TO 1974 REVIEW OF RULES BY STANDING COMMITTEE ON PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter Baker (President of the Privy Council and Minister of National Revenue) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACTS, 1867 TO 1974 REVIEW OF RULES BY STANDING COMMITTEE ON PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS
speechtext:
That the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections be authorized pursuant to section 7, chapter 13. Statues of Canada. 1974-75-76, to review the rules provided by subsection 51(1) of the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1974, as amended by the British North America Act (No, 2), 1974, and to make recommendations with respect to any amendments, alterations or modifications thereto that appear to the committee then to be necessary or desirable.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as you probably know, the reason I am rising today to move this motion is the existence of a provision in the Representation Act of 1974 which obliges me to propose to the House, not later than the twenty-fifth sitting day after Parliament has been summoned, that an order be made along the lines of the motion Your Honour has just read.
1 would emphasize that this does not involve the boundaries of particular constituencies but it is, nevertheless, of fundamental importance to members of the House of Commons because it would affect the number of seats in the chamber. 1 was interested today, as we moved toward this point in our proceedings, to notice that hon. members do raise questions as to their ability to catch the eye of the Chair; I am talking about the period of time in which members, under our rules, can question ministers. We are now up to 282 members in the House of Commons and one of the fundamental questions a committee would have to consider is whether or not membership has grown to the extent to which it ought to grow, whether, indeed, it has already gone beyond that point, and

November 12, 1979
British North America Acts
whether there ought to be some limit placed upon the size of the membership. Considerations of this kind could have a profound effect on the lives of members in terms of the question period, their ability to take part in debates, the staffing of committees, their ability to deal with the public and handle the ombudsman role which they play, and so on.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the British North America Act of 1867 gave Canada its present legislature. The upper House was to consist of 24 non-elected members for each region, Quebec, Ontario and the maritimes, and this representation was to remain constant regardless of changes in the population. The House of Commons, on the other hand, was established on the basis of representation by population and there have, from time to time, been changes in the size of the House as statutes have been amended. Another change was considered necessary when the 1971 census became available, mainly because several provinces would once again return fewer members. That seems to be part of the history of the debates on this subject that take place from time to time.
Under the Representation Act of 1974, Parliament adopted a new set of rules which attempted to compromise between conflicting goals by letting the House grow while setting different rates of increase in the representation of small, intermediate and large provinces. The 1974 rules were applied in the last general election and resulted in a House of 282 seats. Even at the time the rules were being adopted in 1974 there was concern that, depending on the way in which Canada's population grew, the new rules might cause a very rapid increase in the number of seats in the House, and a provision was therefore inserted into the act calling for the referral of the rules to a committee of the House in 1979 in order to permit the examination of the effects of the changes as they would be applied to the 1981 census.
I do not intend to say any more about this motion than 1 already have, Mr. Speaker. I know there are other members who wish to speak with regard to this proposal. Today will not be the only day upon which this matter can be considered, there will be other occasions. But by rising today and proposing this motion 1 have complied with the law and begun the discussion of what I believe to be a fundamental question for every one of us here, that is, whether or not the House is to grow continually, as it has in the past, or whether there is a limit to its size that we ought to consider in terms of its function, the work of its membership and the ability of the membership to carry on their duties in this chamber.
With those few words 1 will subside and allow others to take part in the debate to the extent that it is possible this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome the remarks of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Baker). The bill he spoke of was one of those I worked on when 1 was parliamentary secretary to the then president of the privy council, the hon. member for Cape Breton High-lands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen) and, later, to the former member for Eglinton, the Hon. Mitchell Sharp.
We had serious difficulty in arriving at formulas that would be acceptable to the House of Commons because of the dilemma we face in this country posed by the distribution of population between provinces. There are ten provinces and two territories with tremendous differentials in terms of population, and tremendous differentials in terms of embedded rules. The oldest and perhaps the most important in some respects is the Senate rule which provides Prince Edward Island, for example, with four seats because the rule states that a province cannot have fewer parliamentary seats than it has senators. Consequently, what has happened is that some provinces have maintained their populations while others have grown to the extent that, had a system been in place with a set number of seats, there would need to be a net transfer of seats from some provinces and regions to others.
Consequently, when the first series of proposals was brought down, beginning with one in 1971, the House determined that this was not the best way in which to proceed to the redistribution of parliamentary seats between provinces because those original proposals would have meant certain provinces losing seats. After considerable debate a decision was taken to suspend the operation and new proposals were advanced by the then president of the privy council, the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso, which resulted in the present situation.
As I said earlier, we have a problem in that there are parts of the country which are not growing and parts which are growing rapidly. Moreover, we must face the fact that certain implied guarantees have been given to the regions of this country as to the number of parliamentary seats they would have and as to the influence of those seats. While representation according to population has always been the battle cry of certain groups, it has never been a principle which was fully accepted as being unalterable.
If one goes over the history of the distribution of parliamentary seats in Canada one discovers that the formula of representation by population has never been followed precisely. It has always been the feeling that those areas with large geographic areas and small populations ought to be given more representation in order to compensate. If one goes back over history, one will find that that in fact is what has happened, and that has been carried on with a fair amount of non-partisanship by the members of the political parties in the House of Commons and also with a certain degree of concern as to what happens to those areas which are not growing as fast as other areas.
Since these proposals were developed-the so-called amalgam method-we have had a substantial shift in demographic population development which had been taking place at that time. In those days of 1974-75 it was the province of Ontario which was growing the quickest and, according to what we knew then and to what all the data indicated, it would continue to grow most rapidly. We now know that growth in Ontario has levelled off and that growth in the province of

November 12, 1979

Alberta particularly, but also British Columbia and Saskatchewan, has increased at an extraordinarily rapid rate. We know that growth in Quebec has levelled off, as it has in the province of Ontario.
We know also that if we do not look at the amalgam method, we will have a substantial increase in the number of members of Parliament in the Parliament after this one, and we have to look at what that means to this particular chamber. In comparison with the other place and in comparison with the House of Commons in Great Britain, our chamber is virtually a barn, and it may well be that one of the things we should examine in any event, whether we increase the number of members of the House of Commons or not, is whether this chamber is appropriate to the kind of performance we now put on. I speak of performance because one cannot overcome the feeling in walking on to the floor of this House that we are walking on to a brightly lit theatrical stage, and I think to some extent that brings out the worst in all of us. The fact is that the kind of image that is transmitted by the television cameras is not the kind of image that those of us who practice our magic on the floor of the House of Commons have. There is a discrepancy between what goes on here and what goes out.
I look at it from the point of view that perhaps we should go and look at the way the British have organized their chamber with a view to getting rid of these desks and moving to a more sensible approach-going on to benches and allowing for the fact that we do not need to have space for all the members of the House of Commons, although we do have to have space here for those who want to participate in the debates. If we would like to go to a cosier system than the kind of system where we are spread all over this large barn, I think that is one of the aspects we would have to examine regarding the expansion in the number of members of the House of Commons.
We have absorbed, through the amalgam method, an additional number of members, and if my recollection is correct, after the next redistribution of parliamentary seats as between the provinces we will end up with a total of seats slightly under or slightly over the 300 mark. That would mean a substantial increase in the number of people absorbed into this system in a very brief period of time.
I am not certain that that kind of change would deal adequately with the problems of those of us who represent very large constituencies. In my own case, my constituency was already large before the last redistribution of parliamentary seats, encompassing some 55,000 square miles, but it suddenly blossomed into a monster of 150,000 square miles. What we have seen taking place has been the movement of population from rural areas into cities. We have seen substantial growth in the physical size of rural constituencies, and members of Parliament have extreme difficulty in providing adequate representation to people who in many respects are receiving less representation now than they did before, even though the Canadian public as a whole may in fact be receiving more and better representation as a result of the expansion of the numbers in this place.
British North America Acts
So I agree with the President of the Privy Council that the question of numbers is very important. But not only is the question of numbers important; so is the question of the quality of representation for individual Canadians which will flow out of changes we make to this formula. I think that point has to be our bottom line. What kind of a system of representation do we want for the Canadian people?
The second point I want to make deals with changes in the system we have developed. Whenever we bring in a new system of any nature, some kind of examination is required to discover what in fact happened, and one of the things about the remarks made by the President of the Privy Council which disappointed me was that he did not indicate whether the government would be prepared to provide the committee with the necessary data and breakdown as to the results of what actually happened. We are not interested here in the results of an election. What we are interested in are what the results in terms of the representation of Canadians in general are going to be.
I do not know whether the government has yet appointed a representation commissioner, but I believe that office is still vacant. I think it is one which the government should give some consideration to filling before this investigation goes on, because it strikes me that the committee will be in need of the advice and research capability which that office has. That office has been vacant for about a year, but it does strike me that the committee should undertake to examine whether we should proceed until in fact there is a representation commissioner. 1 urge upon the President of the Privy Council that consideration be given to that aspect.
The last point I want to make is contained in the presentation which was made by the previous president of the privy council when he made a statement to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections on April 9, 1974. I should refer this document to the President of the Privy Council because it was a cabinet document, and cabinet documents often were released in the form of ministerial speeches and papers released to committees and what not; it is not as if they were always kept secret. The fact is that by and large the bulk of the advice and data contained in these papers were made available to members of Parliament and the general public, although not in the form of a cabinet paper. I think many people's concept that they should have access to cabinet papers is that they would like to get into their hot little hands papers stamped "top secret-for the eyes of cabinet ministers only".
1 want to refer to this paper, and I suggest to the President of the Privy Council that it be duplicated and made available to the members of the committee. The reason for that is that the paper not only goes into the historical development of how we got to where we are in terms of the redistribution of parliamentary seats as between provinces, but it also suggests a variety of formulae-in fact, another four formulae in some detail-along with calculations as to what the end result will be in terms of the number of members of this chamber and in terms of what would happen to the various provinces in terms of their representation. I think it would be useful for members

November 12, 1979
British North America Acts
of Parliament to have the advantage of those formulae in their contemplation of our existing one to give them an idea of what the consequences of almost any formula man can devise are.
It is not clear, when we look at the formulae, as to the results we will reap. The fundamental difference I have with those formulae is that they are all based on projections by Statistics Canada as to population trends. We know what has happened in the last five years. Those population trends have been completely thrown out of any match with reality today. The reasons are simple enough. Population is flowing westward, Canadians are not having babies and we have slowed down our intake of immigration. The consequence of that has been to throw into the ashcan all of the Statistics Canada demographic projections. This is not to be critical in any way of Statistics Canada; it is simply an indication of the way in which what appeared to be at the time rather fixed demographic characteristics of a country or region can be changed overnight, and that is what has happened.
The last point 1 want to raise is the question of what happens after we go through this process. We will have to deal at some point with the redistribution of parliamentary seats within provinces. I think we have had a general agreement that the formula which we had developed and accepted, the amalgam method of redistribution of parliamentary seats among provinces, was a broadly accepted formula the last time, but what was not accepted by a large number of Canadians and a large number of members of Parliament then and now was what happened when we redistributed those seats within provinces. What happened then was the grossest kind of distortion, the grossest kind of misappropriation of parliamentary seats that 1 have ever seen. No account or little account was taken of communities and of interests, no account was taken of the sheer geographical size of constituencies, and no account was taken of like interests.
Having gone through the very painful experience of having been one of those whose constituency was changed out of all recognition, sacrificed on the altar of a principle almost as repugnant to most of us as proportional representation-but this one is called equality of representation within a province- I feel most strongly about that. What is so bothersome about it is that when that original act was passed in 1964-65, a formula was inserted to allow the redistribution commission in each province a lot of latitude. There was the possibility of a 50 per cent differential between an urban constituency and a rural constituency, and if you look at the map of Ontario you will find that in almost no case at all was the formula utilized.
One of the biggest mistakes I personally made was when I combined with the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) to pass a private member's bill through the House of Commons-I point that out to the President of the Privy Council-in which we asked the commissioners to give reasons for their decisions so that we could have an opportunity at the public hearings to dispute them, because if we did not have that right there would be no opportunity to challenge their

findings. The bill was passed and my good friend, the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Penner), who was then member for Thunder Bay and whose riding was destroyed by the commissioners, tried to take the matter to court on this point. The result was that because the commissioners had put in a one sentence reason, which in effect said "In our best judgment, this is the best thing with which we can come up", the courts refused to hear the case. It seems to me that we have to do something to ensure that the commissioners carry out the will of Parliament, not what their own interpretation of that will is.
1 would ask the President of the Privy Council if he would be prepared to accept an amendment to this motion to ensure that we do not deal with the issue of redistribution of parliamentary seats by only taking half of it but that we deal with the whole bag, that we deal with the redistribution of parliamentary seats among provinces and that we deal with it also within provinces. Because it is as important to ensure fair representation to the public of Canada as it is to ensure that the workload of members of Parliament with respect to their constituencies is as equalized as it can be. I can tell the President of the Privy Council and the House that right now those members who represent larger constituencies carry a heavier burden than those who represent smaller, more compact interest groups and constituencies, and this is simply not fair.
The hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Pepin) mentions that there are other factors, and of course there are, but I say that the system under which we operate forces many of us into courses that are not desirable or healthy for the people we represent.
So I want to make that plea to the President of the Privy Council and ask him if he would accept an amendment at this stage to include the other act, or if he would give us a guarantee that, at a later time, he would bring down a motion to refer the other act to the standing committee. 1 think it would be healthy, if we must examine one half of the problem, to examine all of the problem. As I said, 1 do not think we should go at it in a half-baked way. 1 think we should look at the whole problem, because we cannot escape the reality of the dimensions of the problem. The two are intertwined and therefore must be examined on that basis.
I think we must examine also one other factor, which is the question of how we should determine in the future what kind of a formula will be most apt. The dilemma that we have when we undertake this examination is that if we should decide to change it, it means that the basis of the representation in the House will have been changed very substantially within a five-year period of time. This means that the continuity which has been built up in constituencies and in areas can be destroyed because in many cases constituencies become used to being referred to as a constituency and they work within the boundaries that the provincial constituency imposes upon them.
What concerns me is that while I welcome the opportunity to re-examine the formulas, 1 have some concern about what we might bring forward as alternative. We might destroy that
November 12, 1979

kind of continuity which, in a political sense, I believe is a very important thing. What makes a political system acceptable and workable and what gives it credibility with the electorate is the fact that people know what to expect. What happened in the last redistribution is that people did not know what to expect, and a great deal of concern was expressed in that sense. I recognize the dilemma we are imposing on ourselves, but 1 belive it is worth exploring this point in second reading debate.
So on that basis I would like to see the President of the Privy Council proceed with the search to find a representation commissioner; that the government produce a fairly substantive paper, perhaps much along the lines of the paper which was produced by his predecessor on April 9, 1974; that consideration be given to expanding the role of the committee to deal with the redistribution of parliamentary seats within provinces; and lastly, that the committee itself give some consideration to the need for continuity.

Mr. Speaker, 1 want to raise a couple of points briefly with reference to this bill. First

November 12, 1979
Borrowing Authority Act
I want to raise a matter which perhaps 1 could have raised as a point of order, but which I think could well be brought forward in the course of my general remarks at this time. It is my understanding that it is customary, before the House proceeds to report stage and third reading of a bill, that there be available to members the printed proceedings of the committee hearings on that measure. As far as I am aware, this is not the case with respect to Bill C-10. When I did not see the printed proceedings of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs in my office, I checked with the clerk of the committee and she informed me that the proceedings setting out the verbatim transcript of the discussions in committee on Bill C-10 have not yet been printed. This information from the clerk of the committee came to my attention approximately half an hour ago.
I am not certain that the rules of the House, or the interpretation of the rules of the House, are so precise that a bill cannot be proceeded with if the printed proceedings of a committee, once it has held hearings on a bill, are not available. However, I think one could agree that certainly it is difficult for members of the House generally to give proper attention to a bill at report stage or third reading without the benefit of the final version of the proceedings of the bill. There may well be members of the House who would like to speak on a bill and who would like to address their minds to the full picture regarding the bill, before making up their minds as to where they stand on it, yet they may not have been members of the standing committee which considered the bill, or even if they were members, they may not have been able to be present to take part in its deliberations.
Frankly I do not think it is consistent with the pledges of the new government in the Speech from the Throne, namely that it would show greater respect for Parliament and enhance the role of Parliament, in particular through increasing the role of parliamentary committees, to proceed as it is doing with respect to Bill C-10. At the very least it shows some degree of contradiction of the high-minded words of the Speech from the Throne, with respect to enhancing the authority of Parliament, to ask the House to proceed to take a final decision on Bill C-10 without members of the House having before them the printed proceedings, the only complete transcript generally available to members of the discussions on Bill C-10 before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
There were some very interesting and useful exchanges in committee between members of the committee, particularly those on the official opposition side, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) with respect to the purpose of the bill and the justification for it. It does not make it easy to debate the bill at this time when one does not have the actual transcript in the form of the final written proceedings. While I am not going to interrupt the proceedings of the House on this bill by raising a formal point of order, 1 want to say that I and members of the official opposition disagree most strongly with this course of conduct. In my view, it flies in the face of the alleged commitment of the new government to enhance the role of Parliament. If a similar occasion arises, speaking for
myself, I can say that I will object most strongly in terms of a formal point of order.
I should like to speak briefly on some of the considerations connected with this bill. In my view at least, and again speaking from my general recollection rather than from the printed transcript of the committee proceedings, the Minister of Finance was not able to give a more convincing justification before the committee for the amount of the borrowing authority he is seeking in this bill than he was able to give in winding up debate on second reading. As the House knows, the bill calls for borrowing authority in the amount of $7 billion. However, in his economic statement of last July, the Minister of Finance said that cash requirements for the period to which this bill relates would be in the amount of $10 billion. The figures given by the minister, both at the end of second reading debate and, more particularly, in committee hearings on this bill, indicate that he is asking for anywhere from $3 billion to $5 billion more than he needs to achieve the borrowing authority necessary to meet the cash requirements he predicted for the current fiscal year.
We pressed the Minister of Finance in committee as to why he needed the very sizeable amount of anywhere from $3 billion to $5 billion more than what appeared to be required. Of course, it depends on how one adds it up-that is, the existing borrowing authority and the new borrowing authority being sought-but he said only that he would need something for contingencies. Those are pretty wide-ranging contingencies, especially coming from a government and a minister which say that they have embarked upon a course of providing more information to Parliament about financial requirements than the previous government, and of being more definite and open with the public and Parliament about the manner in which they handle the financial affairs of the country.
1 want to say to the House that I recall nothing from the committee proceedings which would cause me to change my mind in respect of the conclusion 1 reached on second reading, that there were several billion dollars worth of what I call padding in this borrowing authority bill-moneys being sought for which there was no adequate or convincing explanation.
Of course, one can speculate on what the Minister of Finance had in mind when he spoke of contingencies. One possibility is that his department's own most recent forecast recognized that the economy is going to slow down to such an extent during and before the end of this fiscal year that government revenues will decline sharply, so that additional borrowing authority will be required for the government to borrow in order to meet the gap between revenues and expenses for the current fiscal year.
Another possible explanation for the reference by the Minister of Finance to contingencies is that the government may feel that at some point in the period covered by Bill C-10 it will have to go to international financial markets to borrow extensively to support the dollar. The government may have a view on the value of the dollar. After all, the previous minister of

November 12, 1979

finance said in the House of Commons, if I am not mistaken, that he thought the Canadian dollar should be worth 90 cents. It could be that the minister under the guise of squirrelling money aside, putting it away for contingencies, has in mind some substantial borrowing effort required to support the dollar.
Another possible explanation for the substantial sum the Minister of Finance is seeking to cover contingencies is that if the government proceeds with its misguided intention of breaking up Petro-Canada, our national oil company, giving the money-raising or profitable parts to the public while at the same time keeping not only the money-losing but necessary national interest parts in government hands, and having the government assume the present debt, this would in effect mean, in a technical sense at least, a borrowing by the federal government of the amount of some $2.5 billion, the existing debt of Petro-Canada. This is an additional burden on the taxpayer, for which the taxpayer is getting nothing in return, which would have to be covered by additional borrowing authority.
I would also bring to the attention of the House still another possible explanation for the additional borrowing authority which the Minister of Finance spoke about as being required to cover contingencies which he declined to identify or explain. Because of the high interest rate policy supported, believed in and agreed to by this present government, a policy which has raised interest rates in Canada since May 22 to record high levels, the government itself will have to pay more money to people from whom it has borrowed money in the past, and from whom it is borrowing money now, in the form of increased interest on those borrowings. This would obviously be a lot more than might have been foreseen a year or so ago, and this also has to be covered by the borrowing authority. What is involved in the payment of additional amounts for interest on the government's debt is an additional burden on the Canadian taxpayer. The interest burden is already unfortunately, in my view at least, too high on the Canadian taxpayer in view of the taxpayer's capacity as a consumer, farmer or small business person.
This additional burden will have to be paid in due course by the taxpayer through his or her taxes to cover additional interest expense on government borrowing. There may have to be borrowing to cover this interest in the short run, and this also will have to be covered by the additional borrowing authority sought by Bill C-10.
Even though, as I have said, the Minister of Finance both at second reading and at the committee stage on this bill failed to give a completely convincing response to my questions as to exactly why this borrowing authority is required, particularly the portion that seems to be anywhere from $3 billion to $5 billion more than the cash requirements he said would be required for the current fiscal year, we do not intend to prolong unduly the taking of a final decision on this bill.
I presume the government takes the view that it knows what it is doing. We do not think that is the case. If we let more time go by, this will be demonstrated to the public even more
Borrowing Authority Act
fully than the mistakes, the flip-flops and the lack of action we have seen from this new government in the almost half a year it has been in office to this point in time.
As a result, it is our intention, as I say, not to prolong the debate on this bill unduly, but we do want first of all to protest again that this government, which claimed to be committed to showing greater respect for Parliament and, in particular, for the work of its committees, is asking us to proceed without having available to all members of this House the complete official transcript of the committee proceedings on this bill. This means, as 1 have said, that those members who were not on the committee, or who perhaps do not have a form of recollection at the level or to the extent they would like, are not in the position they should be in order to direct their minds to the issues in connection with this bill. Some of us who were there and were very interested in this bill feel ready to discuss the issues and the gaps in the government's approach to it. However, certainly what the government has done in respect of this bill is not consistent with the way its members say they want Parliament to be treated.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I think we have put enough on the record to indicate that this government, when it was in opposition, complained strongly that the previous government was asking for authority for which it had given no detailed explanation, yet this government is proceeding along the same course of action it criticized in the past. In fact, in my view it is going further in some ways, and I think it should be on the record that there are serious gaps in the justification attempted for this bill by the Minister of Finance.

Mr. Speaker, I am always somewhat bemused when I listen to a speech by the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) on matters of finance. I think the only question the Canadian people should ask themselves when they listen to that hon. member is, would things have been any different had there not been a change as a result of the election of May 22? If that hon. member can honestly go before the Canadian people and say they would have done anything different in respect of Bill C-10 or in respect of interest rates, I suggest he would be asking the Canadian people to buy a bill of goods they are not prepared to accept.
Be that as it may, the hon. member did make one particular point toward the end of his remarks which I think is absolutely true, and that was when he said this government is proceeding in the same direction as the previous government. I am glad he has finally come around to that point of view as that is precisely what we have been saying since the election. There is no difference in the policies followed by the two governments, either from the point of view of the way in which this bill was presented, or in terms of the substance of the government's economic policy which this bill gave us an opportunity to discuss on second reading and again in the committee, albeit during a one-day sitting of that committee.
From the point of view of the way in which this bill was presented, I think the best criticisms were made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) in a speech he made on October 25,

November 12, 1979
Borrowing Authority Act
1978 when he was leader of the opposition. He was most critical of the government at that time for coming before Parliament asking for authority to borrow billions of dollars before the minister of finance of that day had presented a budget. We are now presented with exactly the same situation and exactly the same problem, as an opposition, of looking at a supplemental borrowing authority bill without, at the same time, having the opportunity to discuss the reasons and the objectives of the government's spending program and the reasons and objectives of the government's revenue collecting program.
1 think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) knows full well our concern with respect to tax spending. We have made that clear over a period of months and years. We are looking forward to the budget in which something will be done about that.
We also look forward, Mr. Speaker, to seeing the government's economic intentions outlined in the budget. When the government brings in a bill requesting supplemental authority to borrow substantial sums of money, I think it should done in conjunction with a budget and not before a budget. That would give us the opportunity to look at the economic situation as a whole.
There is a discrepancy between the good intentions of the government, as expressed from time to time, on freedom of information and the answers we get to some of our questions. The Minister of Finance, for example, was not willing to commit himself to changing the practice with respect to a bill of this nature. When we raised with the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) the other day the question concerning privatization and the selling off of certain Crown corporations, we did not get from him a ringing declaration that Parliament would reign supreme in this matter. We did not get a statement from him that he would be glad to debate his objectives with any other member of Parliament in a committee, so that the matter would be discussed. He did not give us an opportunity to bring members of the industry before a committee of the whole Flouse or a committee of the House. No such commitments came from the President of the Treasury Board. All we got was the kind of evasive, arrogant answer that we got from the previous Liberal administration.
It is quite understandable that the President of the Treasury Board is frustrated. Finally he is in government after so many years, but now he says to us, "Why do you expect from us a different standard of behaviour than you got from the Liberals?" That is really what he was telling the people of Canada on Thursday. "Why do you expect anything better from us?"
As a member of the New Democratic Party, I can only nod and ask, "Why indeed?" We do not really expect a diffrent standard of behaviour. It is only that they told us they were going to give us a diffrent standard of behaviour. I suggest to those members of the Conservative party who are present that they might care to bring their alleged desires with respect to the authority of Parliament in matters of this nature in line
with their conduct, which still has a long way to go. Of course, it is difficult to do this. It demands a change in government and a change in attitude on the part of the civil service, but I think we expect a little more indication from ministers of the Crown at this time of the direction they intend to take.
Two or three other interesting things were said during debate on second reading and the committee discussions which I think are worth commenting upon. For the first time, we had in that committee a new language coined by the Minister of Finance. For example, he said that the Conservative party does not have a high interest policy; that the Conservative party inherited a high interest condition for which it accepts no responsibility. That was an interesting, rhetorical attempt by the minister to avoid taking responsibility, a natural psychological move on his part. It was a very clever, rhetorical trick.
Then he tried something else. He told us that previously a stimulative deficit, temporary or not, had meant a larger deficit and that he was now defining a stimulative deficit as meaning a smaller deficit. That is a very interesting idea. It was an effort to ignore the albatross which had hung around his neck since the election. One can only admire the minister's efforts to get around the difficulties created for him by his colleagues.
In this party, however, we are not going to allow the Minister of Finance to invent this new language in order that he and the Government of Canada can avoid responsibility for the economic policies now being followed. 1 think we have seen an interesting, psychological game being played since the recall of Parliament. On the one hand, we have an official opposition which has yet to accept its role as an opposition. Psychologically it still sees itself as the government. It cannot get used to the fact that other people are acting as ministers, going to cabinet meetings and taking responsibility for the direction of the country. After 16 years of power you get used to it, so there is a certain complacency built into the arteries of members of the Liberal party. One can understand their withdrawal symptoms, which are expressed in various forms.
The hon. member for Windsor West, for example, expresses his withdrawal symptoms by acting as if he were not a member of the Liberal party prior to May 22. According to him, the Liberal party sprang immaculate from his loins on May 23, and everything in place before then was out of some movie in which he played no part.
Where did you come from?
My origins are a matter of history.
Where is all the Max Saltsman philosophy?
He is a test tube baby.

1 do not think it will wash with the people of Canada. They remember seeing the hon. member for Windsor West on television when he was minister of consumer and corporate affairs. They remember him very well when he was minister of national revenue and they vividly remember his role as chairman of the finance committee in the dark days of

November 12, 1979

1969-70. The hon. member for Windsor West has a history. He cannot pretend he came here on May 23 and invented the Liberal party, it has a history too, and that history is precisely the condition out of which we are trying to emerge with the new government which sits across the way.
if the Liberal party has its psychological problems, I suggest to members of the Conservative party, and particularly to the Minister of Finance who is not here this afternoon, that they, too, have their psychological problem. They still do not see themselves as a government. Every time the Minister of Finance gets up to answer a question, all he can say is "We cannot do 'X', we canot do *Y\ we cannot do 'Z' because of the Liberal party, because of the Liberal party, because of the Liberal party." He will not even admit that when he raises interest rates, that is a policy; he says it is a condition. When he does something it is a condition; when anybody else does it, it is a policy. It is interesting blarney, interesting rhetoric, but 1 suggest it will not wash. It just is not good enough.
We are waiting eagerly for the budget, Mr. Speaker. We are waiting eagerly for the time when we no longer have "Cros-bie's complaint" or "Crosbie's lament", but when we have "Crosbie's budget". He has indicated that this week he will announce the date of the budget. At that point the Conservative party will no longer be able blindly to blame somebody else for the problems of the country. They have to take some responsibility for what happens. They are slowly building themselves a record-in my view an uneven record-and at some stage the Minister of Finance is going to have to take responsibility and recognize that he cannot blame high interest rates on somebody else forever. Neither can he blame large deficits on somebody else forever. The Minister of Finance will have to recognize that he has the ability to cancel or change whatever government program he wants, that he has full authority to raise whatever money he wants to deal with whatever budgetary deficit he sees. The Minister of Finance has that power. We in Parliament have that power.
Just as the whole of "Portnoy's Complaint" was a prelude to serious analysis and rebirth, I suggest that "Crosbie's complaint" and all the falderal that we have heard from the government with respect to high interest rates and economic policies is merely a prelude to what we hope will be the government's coming to accept responsibility and to recognize that it has the reins of power. It is up to the government to act in the way they want, to do the things they want and to address themselves to the problems of the country.
With respect to Bill C-10, 1 suggest that this demands two things. First, that we no longer have requests for borrowing which are completely unrelated to any existing government program. We do not know what the government intends to do with Petro-Canada. We do not know what the debt will be that the government will assume when it sells off the profitable parts of PetroCan. We had no indication from the minister at that time. He said that it was hypothetical and purely speculative.
Borrowing Authority Act
We know the government intends to go ahead with the mortgage interest plan. We know how much that will cost, or what the government thinks it will cost, but again we do not know what other measures the government intends to enact, so how can I say yea or nay to a bill requesting $7 billion?
If debate on this bill has seemed rather empty, shallow and short as it has gone on, there is a simple reason for it. We do not have the material, the economic planning or effort from the government telling us in which direction to move.
On the substantive side as opposed to the procedural side, we hope the government will take some responsibility also. As I said before in all sincerity, there is a contrast-and I will put it no higher than that because this is a young government, and governments and ministers can learn and respond to criticism which I am sure they are getting from members of their own party and from us. It is no longer good enough to come into this House and say that something that was good enough for the Liberal party is good enough for them. If the Liberals did the same thing, we on this side of the House have no right to complain.
1 simply point out to the President of the Treasury Board that we complained along with him, when the Liberals were in power. We intend to do exactly the same thing with respect to information, debate, the fundamental authority of parliament and its committees for questions of supply and economic policy, just as we did then. We look forward to working with the government. We look forward to the budget when it comes, and we look forward to providing the government with constructive criticism, which I hope its members will agree we have attempted to give since the beginning of Parliament. We have set high standards. We have standards which were set in a sense by the Conservative party and by members such as the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) when in opposition. Those standards are: that a government minister will answer questions directly when asked, that he will not attempt to slough them off and that before we are asked to approve billions of dollars of borrowing authority we will have greater financial information on which to base our assent or dissent.

Mr. Chairman, we agreed today that we would discuss regional development policy with the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. 1 believe this is the first opportunity that the minister has had to be here, apart from the standing committee, although I am not sure of that. The Minister of Finance has participated and he was, of course, a most competent replacement. However, we welcome the opportunity of being able to discuss regional development and the matter of DREE with the minister.
We are very happy that a member from Nova Scotia was appointed minister of DREE. Our only regret is that he is not a member of the inner cabinet. As he knows, we sympathize with him in that respect. As a matter of fact, I moved a motion under Standing Order 43 not long ago in that regard. I am sure he would have agreed with my motion, but someone on his side disagreed. Therefore, he cannot be a part of the inner cabinet. Nevertheless, we are sure he will be a good member of the economic development committee or whatever it is called.
My speech will not be long because other colleagues want to speak before five o'clock, after eight o'clock tonight, tomorrow and possibly the day after.
There are a few questions I would like to raise with the minister having to do with my own area. My colleague, the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane, on another occasion will speak on behalf of our party.
Can the minister tell us whether his department has initiated discussions with the province of New Brunswick on a highways agreement to continue the work started by the previous government and the province of New Brunswick? When I say with the province of New Brunswick, I must mention that the province has not done that much. It was mostly federal money that went on routes 11, 8 and 17 in northeastern New Brunswick. To sum up my first question, it is this: Have discussions been initiated on a new highways agreement with the province of New Brunswick covering routes 11,8 and 17?
Second, regarding the DREE northeast New Brunswick agreement, if the minister does not have the figures with him, could he give us a commitment to give the House a report as to the disbursement of funds under that DREE northeast agreement? Up to July or August of this year funds were not being
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Scott, Victoria-Haliburton).]
spent as fast as contemplated. There were goods reasons at the time for that. Some had to do with problems regarding the shipping and marine museum. That was delayed for reasons outside policy decisions of both governments. Another reason was major projects by municipal and industrial infrastructures in Bathurst. Again there were delays because of engineering on the part of the city and so on.
I would like the minister to attempt to give an assessment now and for the rest of this fiscal year as to whether there will be a catch-up in the spending of funds that has been agreed to by both governments, because the government will end in 1982. That means there are two full fiscal years after this year. I am concerned. I would not want any projects foreseen in the agreement to be abandoned.
I know it will be said that Treasury Boards, federal and provincial, could agree to extend the agreement so that the funds can be disbursed. 1 remind the minister that because of inflation, if something is not gone ahead with before the end of the agreement in 1982, unless it is for ongoing projects, tenders called or projects already under construction, it would be difficult to get an extension of the agreement. They would not approve enough money to cover all the projects. That concerns me.
I will wait for the minister's assessment. 1 want his assurance that he will do all he can to approve projects as quickly as possible. 1 hope he will press the New Brunswick government to go forward with projects and ensure that this money will be spent. Before continuing, I would like the minister to answer those two questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
subsubtopic: APPROPRIATION ACT NO. 1-1979-80
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am happy to make myself available to the hon. member and do the best I can to respond to his questions. According to my information, the highway subagreement to which he refers expires March 31, 1980. We have been talking to the province of New Brunswick about extending it. Implicit in this is an additional $5 million or $6 million to be advanced, as I understand it.
I should tell the hon. member that I had an opportunity during the summer to meet with Premier Hatfield and his cabinet and to discuss a number of matters, including the vital forest industry which is important for the entire province of New Brunswick. 1 believe there is approximately half a billion dollars directly or indirectly involved in the New Brunswick economy with the forest industry.
The New Brunswick minister, Mr. Merrithew, was recently here and I met with him outside the chamber. They are still evaluating the various considerations that will eventually, and I think soon, enable them to come forward with some precise proposals so that we can use our pulp and paper agreement to help them rationalize and modernize some of the facilities there.
Another project the hon. member asked about was the shipping and marine centre. That was mentioned in his first question. He knows that a New Brunswick firm, A. C. Mallet
November 12, 1979

& Sons, were awarded a contract. It came in over cost. Negotiations are going on to see how we can best handle it in view of the fact it is a good project. However, the project may require some modifications because of the cost variations between what was envisioned and the tenders.
Something else the hon. member was referring to in northern New Brunswick was the possible zinc reduction plant at Belledune. As he knows, there is an agreement involving this with, as 1 remember, DREE paying $1.6 million, the New Brunswick Mining and Smelting paying approximately the same amount and the New Brunswick government contributing a percentage as well.
As the hon. member knows, the various subagreements in New Brunswick are extensive. They are all under negotiation. We hope that in the not too distant future we will be able to extend the mandate and rationalize the basis of regional development. We will be bringing legislation forward. At the present time, the province of New Brunswick is showing a great deal of interest in all of these subagreements. I am not aware of any serious problems in disbursing funds. There may be.
As the hon. member knows, under the general development concept of DREE which his government brought forward in 1974 there is a fair amount of flexibility with regard to priorities under the general umbrella agreement. We certainly would not object to the province changing some of its priorities if it felt it would be best to expend some of the funds on one subagreement as distinct from another. I want to assure the hon. member that I am not aware of any problem with funds lapsing or not being properly utilized. If there were, I would be concerned about it. 1 would want to get more information and to ensure that the funds were spent as envisaged.
