Mr. Chairman, the minister referred to two projects under the DREE northeast agreement. Under the northeast subsidiary agreement, funds are not being disbursed as was foreseen. 1 can well understand that the minister would not be aware of every detail in these matters. After all, it is administrative and he is still relatively new to the department. 1 assure him that has not been a problem up until now in the sense that no projects that were foreseen have been abandoned. However, it will become a problem. As of last July, 1 received an assessment from officials of his department to the effect that if the trend continues and there is not a speed up of the administration of the agreement, projects that were foreseen could not begin and be completed by March 1982 or July 1982 when the agreement expires. That is the DREE northeast agreement which is different from the highways agreement.
1 would like the minister to inquire from his officials as to the present status and to provide me with a report. 1 do not expect that report in this debate, but I would like it on record that he will ask for it.
[ Translation]
Mr. Chairman, the minister stated that there was now a subsidiary agreement with respect to New Brunswick roads under which major projects have been undertaken on highway
Supply
11, highway 17, and highway 8. In addition, funds have been made available for other secondary roads. This agreement, as the minister said, will be ending on March 31, 1980.
1 would like to ask the minister to make sure in his discussions with New Brunswick that priorities for federal funds will be highway 11, highway 17 and highway 8 for the simple reason that the entire economy of northern New Brunswick from the northwest, the link between Maine, northwest New Brunswick and northeast New Brunswick and the link between the northeast and the Fredericton area, that is highway 8 and the link between the northeast and the Moncton area, for the economy of northeast of New Brunswick, it is extremely important because highway 17, as I said a while ago, provided a link between Maine and the northeast for the tourist industry but it also helps make more effective the transport of our goods coming from central Canada.
As for highway 8 which links northeastern New Brunswick from Fredericton with the whole northeastern part of the United States, that is the Boston area, our lumber especially, our fish and our peat all travel on it by truck. That highway is in terrible shape at this time, which makes the transportation of our goods less efficient than that in other parts of the country which sell the same products.
So I should like to ask the minister to ensure first of all that additional credits are authorized, as he mentioned a while ago, to supplement the present agreement and project, because it is extremely important for the economy of northeastern New Brunswick, the Miramichi area and that part of New Brunswick, to have an adequate network of highways, because we cannot bank on the province to supply the funds required; it simply does not have the financial capacity to supply the $200 million required in 1979. In addition, and my colleague for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) will have more to say about this later on this evening, the province of New Brunswick does not give any priority to road building in that area.
We find that they are building a bridge in the city of Fredericton at a cost of some $25 million to $30 million, who knows? That is more than the province spent on building highways 11, 17 and 8 together. So we cannot expect the province of New Brunswick to do that work. I therefore urge the minister to see to it that the federal government signs another agreement after March 31, 1980, for the construction of roads in that part of the province, making sure that, in its negotiations with the province of New Brunswick, highways 11,8 and 17 are given some priority in the allocation of federal funds.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I do not intend to express my views right now on the remarks just made by the minister regarding a corridor road through the state of Maine. Eventually 1 would like to discuss this question, but I have other major concerns which in my opinion should be given priority. 1 will discuss later the question of the corridor road through Maine.
Today, I had the opportunity, when putting a question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), to complain about the fact that the Canadian Transport Commission will subsidize the VIA Rail to provide a passenger train service through the state of Maine at the very time when they are taking away what was left to us in terms of passenger trains between Edmundston and central Canada via Quebec City. There is something wrong there.
So I will deal with the matter of the corridor road later on. For the time being, 1 would like to congratulate the minister. First, I wish to congratulate him on the honour bestowed on him by being appointed Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. I appreciate that honour because, like him, 1 come from the Atlantic region. My first loyalty is to Canada and then to the area I represent in the House. I wish him every success in his heavy responsibilities which, I am sure, he has already tackled resolutely.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the specific matter I wish to raise with the minister is that of the developing regions sub-agreement entered into by his predecessor, the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Lessard), and the premier of New Brunswick, Mr. Richard Hatfield. Some last minute changes were made to that agreement to comply with certain requirements,- which 1 find excessive, made by the president of the treasury board of New Brunswick who is also the member for the city of Edmundston which I represent in this House. It was understood that the federal government would provide some funds, namely an amount of $1 million, within the framework of that developing regions subagreement, to further upgrade and extend the regional airport landing strip which has been under construction for the past few years in St. Leonard in northwestern New Brunswick. The provincial premier replied that if the agreement did not include moneys for a parking lot in the city of Edmundston in relation to the development of a downtown complex including government offices, a hotel and a
shopping centre, he would not let the province share on a 20 per cent basis the ongoing development of the St. Leonard airport. Faced with that situation, the former minister, the present member for Lac-Saint-Jean, had to agree with the province that if the amount of $1 million could not be allocated to extend the airport it would not be spent either on a parking lot related to the development of the downtown complex. Such was the situation during the election. But I want to remind the minister that the agreement was indeed signed some ten days before the election was held.
You know what happened, and the minister's party is now in power. However, the municipalities in the area which were to be the first to benefit from this agreement, an agreement which provided large amounts of money mainly for water and sewage systems, suffered throughout the summer, because during that period they were told that it was not possible to implement the agreement. It was alleged that the necessary funds were not available this year. I therefore ask the minister to confirm whether this is the case, although I have been told that over $1 million could be spent this year to implement the agreement.
Of course, the northwestern area of Madawaska-Victoria was not the only one which was to benefit from this development agreement, because the Northumberland-Miramichi constituency of the hon. member who is listening to me now was supposed to benefit also from the economic windfalls provided under this agreement.
As far as I know, in spite of the urge of Mr. Simard, president of the treasury board for the province of New Brunswick, to sign this agreement right away and sooner if possible, for all practical purposes it has been shelved for the five or six months since it has been signed. And now 1 am told that some deals were made to withdraw from the agreement the $1 million provided for accelerated construction of the airport and that this sum will be allocated to other projects. Of course, it is quite an embarrassing situation for a minister who inherits a portfolio whose problems were not specifically caused by his own lack of goodwill. My second question to the minister deals with the remarks he has just made in answering my colleague for Gloucester (Mr. Breau). He said that he would not object if the province changed its priorities. I agree with that because certainly the province has the right to modify its priorities and as much as possible the federal government should respect them. But I wonder, Mr. Chairman, what is more important in the global approach of a regional plan concerned with the well-being of a population and its economic progress.
Is it more important for this region to have a city parking lot or the airport facilities it has been requesting since time immemorial? That is where the province's priorities have gone. Since the minister's predecessor had clearly established that the airport was more important than a parking lot it seems to me that any minister should feel compelled to intervene and remind the province that we also have initiating powers. We

November 12, 1979

have the right to initiate projects, the right to say that in our view one project has priority over another which the province might want to sell us. If we do not reserve this prerogative, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that we are completely distorting the very meaning of federal-provincial negotiations. It is the very spirit of development agreements which is at stake here and which could disintegrate. 1 would like the minister to say whether he agrees with me that the federal government has initiating powers. If not, Mr. Chairman, 1 think that a number of us have wasted our time over the last few years. I believe the minister will say that in many cases we do have not only the right to inspect but also the right to criticize. But since we bear 75 per cent or 80 per cent if not more, if not 100 per cent of the cost of those agreements, at some point we must reserve the right to close the gate and say that is our final decision, we want you, our provincial partners, to accept our priority this time, since we are asking you to contribute only 20 per cent.
Before resuming my seat, Mr. Chairman, 1 would like to deal briefly with another development sub-agreement, this one on agriculture. 1 was happy to see the recent opening of an agricultural information centre in the riding south of mine. Mr. Chairman, that will doubtless be very beneficial to agriculture, but in my view, it will not solve a vast number of basic agriculture-related problems in New Brunswick. That agreement provided for the development-funds were even allocated to that effect-for the creation of an agricultural school for the French-speaking people of New Brunswick.
Though new studies have been made on that matter, as far as I know nothing, absolutely nothing, has been decided so far and I understand that if the whole project seems to be in limbo it is because there seems to be disagreement on the specific nature and the site of that training school for young Frenchspeaking farmers.
Well, I for one want not only to express my view in favour of that school for young French-speaking farmers but also to urge the minister to consider that matter as soon as possible, provided he has had no occasion to do it yet, in order to hasten the development of that institution. If that is not done, if the implementation of the project is further postponed, then it is the over-all agricultural sector of New Brunswick which is going to suffer from such failure. Agriculture is not exclusive to the southern part of the province. It is a trade on which hundreds of people in New Brunswick depend, no matter which region they live in.
So I must insist now on the extremely urgent nature of that problem, given the difficult situation in which potato farming has been plunged in recent years, a situation which has not been caused only by the potato industry itself but also by external factors. 1 have talked enough for the moment, Mr. Chairman, and I will give the minister an opportunity to answer my questions.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY PARLIAMENTARY REPRESENTATION
REQUEST FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY PARLIAMENTARY REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
That a Special Joint Committee of the Senate and of the House of Commons be appointed to consider proposals which would have the effect of allocating a [The Deputy Chairman.]
number of additional members of Parliament at large to each party on the basis of the total number of votes received;
That 15 members of the House of Commons, to be designated at a later date, be members on the part of this House on the Special Joint Committee;
That the committee have power to appoint from among its members such subcommittees as may be deemed advisable and necessary and to delegate to such subcommittees all or any of their powers except the power to report directly to the House;
That the committee have power to report from time to time, to send for persons, papers and records, and to examine witnesses and to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be ordered by the committee;
That the quorum of the committee be 12 members, whenever a vote, resolution or other decision is taken, so long as both Houses are represented and that the joint chairmen be authorized to hold meetings, to receive evidence and authorize the printing thereof, when 7 members are present so long as both Houses are represented; and
That a Message be sent to the Senate requesting that that House do unite with this House for the above purpose, and to select, if the Senate deems it to be advisable, members to act on the proposed Special Joint Committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the pleasure it gives me to rise in this House for the first time in a pitched debate since my return after an absence of seven years is all the greater as this subject is closely related to my previous occupation of co-chairman of the Task Force on Canadian Unity.
On November 5, in reply to my question about the approach to constitutional reform and the action needed to define and achieve a renewed federalism, the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) said:
I hope he-
-the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton-
-intends to release-
-he meant "to make"-
-positive and concrete proposals during the coming months, as he has done in the past-
That was very nice of him. As a matter of fact, the proposal I am making today aims at achieving greater unity among Canadians. It is therefore at the request of the right hon. Prime Minister himself that I rise today, and I would like to warn his Progressive Conservative colleagues that he will be furious if he learns that my motion was rejected.
As hon. members will know, this is not a new idea. It even appears among the recommendations made by the Task Force on Canadian Unity in its first report entitled A Future Together, Se retrouver. Several concrete formulas have been submitted in the last ten years by well known political experts like Fox, Cairns, Irvine and others, and by at least one politician, the present leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent).
November 12, 1979

The whole philosophy and mechanics have just been combined in a most useful small book by William P. Irvine under the title: "Does Canada Need A New Electoral System"? I would like to quote the first sentence in the foreword to that book:

Canada's central institutions face a crisis of representation. This has led to a marked loss of legitimacy and hence authority of the federal cabinet, the federal Parliament and the federal judiciary. They are less able to carry through the kinds of accommodation necessary if the country is to survive.
[ Translation]
This is proof enough of the importance of the issue. 1 also note with pleasure that the press is increasingly interested in the issue, which indeed is now more or less in. I shall not insist on the details of the formula for selecting members of Parliament over and above those now .elected under the majority rule, one per constituency. The subject is more complex. I would simply like to indicate my preference, and in my view the detailed work, the discussion and research should be made in committee, where I suggest we should be guided by experts. 1 have no intention either to bore the House with statistics. Everything is in Irvine's book, including a preliminary analysis of the 1979 elections in terms of the effects of the current act. 1 shall mainly and mostly limit myself to a review of the implications of the current electoral system for this country's unity, and the advantages of the measure I am proposing.
1 do not feel, Mr. Speaker, there is any need to recall at this point the importance of political parties in the process of arriving at a consensus over a country's objectives and the major ways of attaining them. I mention this because I would like to put on record some comments by my friend Ron Watts, principal of Queen's University and my colleague on the Task Force on Canadian Unity, one of Canada's leading experts on federal institutions. Dr. Watts stated in an article and I quote:

- in those federations where a parliamentary executive has been adopted, as in Canada, the major responsibility for generating a consensus among the diverse linguistic and cultural groups falls upon the political parties. It is true that in other federations political parties play a fundamental role in aggregating the varied internal interests but, in such federations as the United States and Switzerland, the separation of powers between different central institutions provides a framework of checks and balances which require the majority to take account of minority viewpoints. In the parliamentary system, however, all central power is concentrated in the majority which commands both the legislature and the executive. It is within the parties themselves, therefore, that minority viewpoints must make an impression if they are to have any impact on central policy at all. Apart from the desire to capture the majority of seats in the popular house, there is little in the parliamentary framework of the institutions that forces politicians to look for compromises.
Mr. Watts gives an illustration of federations where this role of the parties has failed. He mentions a number of them, such as Nigeria, Rhodesia and Nyasaland as well as the West Indies. He gives a number of countries where, in his opinion, it has been a success, namely, India and Malaysia. But the importance of the point he is making should be obviously, namely, that in a parliamentary system in a federation, political parties have a tremendous role to play in fostering and
Parliamentary Representation
massaging the consensus that is essential to the unity of these countries.
[ Translation]
It is therefore incumbent upon Canada's political parties to create, as 1 said, the necessary compromises on duality, and regionalism in particular. Do they do this? Does the electoral system help or hinder them? Such is the theme I would like to deal with this afternoon. It is still too early in my view to conclude that Canadian political parties have failed to look for and invent these compromises. Personally this is not my belief. Irvine has this to say, and I quote:

It is not the case, in Canada, that conflicts of interest between English and French Canadians are so intense that parties cannot get votes from both camps.

And I think that the same conclusion applies to regionalism. There still is regional representation in the larger parties, in the three parties 1 have in mind. The two larger parties still have a Pan-Canadian basis and the third is making progress at the regional level. However, and I call on the patriotism of my colleagues and their intelligence, this dualistic and regional representation basis has shrunk in the last election at least in the case of the two main parties. And particularly the result of the last election in terms of the geographic location of the seats gained by the political parties implies a significant polarization of the vote according to regions and languages.
Yet, it is not the vote which is polarized as much as the distribution of seats.
Those are the facts. 1 do not have time to quote everything but the situation of every party is very well analysed by Mr. Irvine. However, the blunt fact of which my colleagues are perfectly aware is that with 14 per cent of votes the Progressive Conservative Party obtained only two seats in Quebec which is only 2.3 per cent of the representation. In 1974, with 19.5 per cent of the vote in Quebec it obtained three seats which is 4 per cent of representation. This is an abnormal, regrettable and dangerous situation. At the same time in 1979, the Liberal party obtained only three seats west of the Ontario-Manitoba border, which is 4 per cent of the seats, even though it got 22.6 per cent of the vote.
Consequently, a part of the public believes that our political parties have already lost their national dimension and you often find those words in newspapers and on the lips of otherwise very intelligent people. And the concerned public fears that the process has already started. Then, Mr. Speaker, maybe this is becoming true or at least this is an impression that should be corrected as soon as possible for the sake of our survival as a nation as impressions are extremely important in that area.
Then, whatever the importance of the other aspects of the constitutional reform-the distribution of powers, the Senate, the Supreme Court, the amending formula, the repatriation,

November 12, 1979
Parliamentary Representation
the protection of basic rights and so on-the reform of our election legislation might be even more urgent than all the other aspects 1 have just mentioned.
What is this reform? What is this notice of motion which 1 am introducing today? People know that our plurality single member system, our "winner in each riding takes all" system which has obvious advantages, particularly in terms of executive stability, tends to over-represent the largest party in each province and countrywide. We all know that this system tends to under-represent the second party and seriously under-represent third parties with dispersed popular support. That does not apply to our friends in le parti Credit Social du Canada.
1 have already indicated in national unity terms how dangerous this was, but the task force on unity said it in so many words. At page 105 the first report reads as follows:
The simple fact is that our elections produce a distorted image of the country, making provinces appear more unanimous in their support of one federal party or another than they really are.
It continues, a few lines later:
Under our current electoral system, which gives the leading party in popular votes a disproportionate share of parliamentary scats in a province, the regional concentration in the representation of political parties is sharply accentuated. This makes it more difficult for a party's representation in the House of Commons to be broadly representative of all the major regions.
In a country as diverse as Canada, this sort of situation leads to a sense of alienation and exclusion from power.
Adequate representation for some provinces, some regions, or one of the two main cultural groups is denied to some political parties-that should be deplored strongly-in spite of the fact that these parties attracted substantial numbers of votes in these provinces, regions or cultural groups. The whole thing downgrades the representative capacity of caucuses and the whole process of party policy formulation. Also it downgrades the representative capacity of cabinet for the party which is in power, and the legitimacy and credibility of the central government itself. In my view it might lead to an over-decentralization of federation which otherwise might have been avoided. With respect to cabinet, the present situation forces the government in some ways to use means to correct this system which puts most parliamentarians ill at ease. Of course, I am referring to inter-party transfers and to appointment to cabinet from the Senate. More generally, parties with truncated caucuses are prevented from doing their jobs as consensus developers, and to me that is tragic.
What is the remedy? The perfect system does not exist. Irvine said it very well, that no system is perfectly even-handed to all parties. The best system is the one that best suits the particular needs of a country at a particular time in its development, as Aristotle would say. At this particular moment national unity is a major preoccupation. Among academics in particular and some politicians, it is generally believed that a mix of the single member plurality system which has the advantages of simplicity, tradition and, as Irvine stated, "cements the link between constituent and representa-

tive" and produces a more effective government, with a proportional representation list system which would ensure fairer representation to regions and minorities, is what Canada needs. I repeat, it would be a combination of constituency members of the House of Commons and at-large members, or national or provincial members. That is what is referred to as "dual representation".
Various proposals have been made. Some add at-large members to the present composition of the House. Other propositions reduce the present number, in order to make room for a greater number of at-large members. The at-large membership would have a great number of advantages. As I said, it would ensure a more adequate representation from all regions and the two main cultural groups in party caucuses and cabinet. Consequently it would increase the sensitivity of parties to regional and minority views. It could help parties develop links with interest groups which are important provincially and nationally. It could encourage parties to campaign everywhere, instead of concentrating on some ridings in order to obtain more seats with fewer votes, which is done sometimes.
Also it could improve the diversity, the specialization and the stability of political personnel and help develop a cadre of experienced politicians. It could help to broaden leadership professionally and geographically. It could contribute to the efficiency and the morale of party organization. It could ensure a better control of bureaucracy. I could go on; the advantages are quite numerous.
There is friendly opposition to my motion; they will oppose it. I expect that. Generally speaking, the arguments invoked will be those against proportional representation, encouragement of ideological dispersion, multiplication of parties, formation of regional parties, more power to third parties, formation of minority governments or that sort of thing. That is what I expect. For those of you who will, would you kindly allow me to recommend that you think about this further and that you also read Irvine, because these consequences are not necessarily so-"they ain't necessarily so", as the song goes.
I want to emphasize also that my recommendation would be for a rather small number of at-large members. As you may know, the task force on unity recommended 60. When members attack the proposition in the motion I hope they will not feel too pleased with themselves because it may be that a further reading, and some of my colleagues have admitted this, will convince them that my motion "ain't" that crazy.
Professor Irvine mentions four conditions that would bring members of this House to change their minds, and this is going to be my last paragraph. They would shock them into it, as he suggests. These four elements are: a sustained period of minority government, and we have had that; the NDP holding the balance of power; substantial erosion of the Liberal vote in Quebec by third parties; and a heightening of the English-French polarization in the House of Commons. I suggest that we have already experienced conditions one and four at least.
November 12, 1979

May I also suggest that we do not wait until we have experienced all four because it might then be too late.
Mr. Irvine suggested it is possible that the situation might require political parties to rise above self-interest. 1 will end on that note, Mr. Speaker, because that is a good quotation. I hope my colleagues will do that. 1 offer now the possibility of sending the matter to the committee where these matters would be discussed and experts heard. It seems to me that the motion is in the national interest, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY PARLIAMENTARY REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 notice that other members would like to get into this debate, so may I say to them at the outset that my remarks will be very brief.
One of the reasons for my brevity, but also for my wanting to say what is on my mind, is that my leader, the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), supports very strongly the principle placed before this House this afternoon by the Hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Pepin), and on an appropriate occasion will present the case as he sees it.
Indeed, as my friend the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton will recall, my leader appeared before the Pepin-Robarts task force and presented this very idea, namely, that we should have in this House of Commons a mix of the single member plurality system and a dose of proportional representation. As I say, my leader will develop this on a later occasion, so it is not necessary for me to do more now than say to the sponsor of this motion that his idea is not as crazy as some of its opponents may suggest.
We in this country quite frankly do have quite a problem in achieving a balance among the regions and the various groups. We have a very difficult problem in connection with proportional representation as among the provinces where we have two, three or four provinces that are large and growing, the other six or seven provinces being smaller. As the hon. member has pointed out, every election produces a result in which the party that gets the largest number of seats has a percentage of the seats in the House much larger than its percentage of the votes. It works down so that the second party may come out fairly close to its percentage, though even it can be short, and the third party and the fourth party can be way down. As a matter of fact, to put it in precise terms, if we had the number of seats in this House that our percentage of votes in the last election warranted, we would be about twice as many as we are. I hope that does not put it into the minds of some members that they should oppose this motion. Certainly we support the general idea that neither a House completely on the basis of single member plurality nor a House completely on the basis of proportional representation would work in Canada. What we need is a mix of the two.
There are many countries, especially in western Europe, that have mixes of this kind. We have experimented at times with this a bit in provincial terms, both in Manitoba and in Alberta.
I strongly support the suggestion of the mover of this motion that this should be studied very carefully and very thoroughly.
Parliamentary Representation
As 1 say, I am going to sit down now so that other members can speak, but I did want to remind my friend that this idea was proposed, no doubt by others, but certainly to the Pepin-Robarts task force by the hon. member for Oshawa. He also proposed it in this House in the context last session of the debate about the Senate. In fact, it was his suggestion that instead of replacing the Senate we have now with the kind of "House of the Federation'' proposed by the former government, it might be better to abolish that place and bring in to this House a number selected on a regional and proportional basis. At any rate, that case will be made later by my leader. In the meantime, I indicate our support of the principle of this resolution and I express the hope that the hon. member has the support of his own party as well.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY PARLIAMENTARY REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by mentioning that the mover of the motion, the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Pepin), was kind enough to send me a monograph of the book "Does Canada Need a New Electoral System?" by Professor Irvine. I have taken the opportunity of reading through it and of considering the arguments that Professor Irvine puts forward. As the hon. member will know, he sets out as well some of the traditional arguments that have been posited against his eventual recommendation, and I want to address some of those during my time today.
1 also appreciate that as one reviews the various motions and bills which have been put before this House, one will see that very few of them are designed to improve and have the purpose of improving Parliament as an institution. 1 think that is a shame because I am persuaded that Canada's institution of Parliament very much needs improvement in terms of representation, in terms of effectiveness and in terms of efficiency. I am not so sure this motion addresses those particular shortcomings of this Parliament, but I want to mention a little more about that as I go on.
In addition, I have been distressed in this House at the exceedingly high degree of partisanship which is exhibited, no matter what issue is under discussion, and I have a feeling that the effect of the motion could be to exacerbate the degree of partisanship which prevails from time to time. Many members I think are more interested in scoring political points than addressing the issues at hand.
When we consider Parliament, we must, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has pointed out, and whether we like it or not, include the Senate, which is an integral part of the parliamentary system in this country.
While the motion addresses the House of Commons alone, I want to say a word about the other place as a part of the parliamentary process. It seems strange to me that no one ever seems to be very happy with the situation of the other place. As one looks over historical documents, it seems strange as well that no one, other than, maybe, the incumbents of the other place, has been happy with it. Throughout the 11 years of the previous administration the then prime minister, now

November 12, 1979
Parliamentary Representation
the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau), spent a considerable amount of time talking about ways and means of reforming the Senate. Despite all the discussions, all the papers and all the propositions put forward, the position at the end of his tenure was the same as it was in 1968 when he became prime minister.
Prior to the last election, the various parties presented papers on the question. This party, now the government, presented a paper entitled "The House of the Provinces", the Liberal party presented a paper entitled "The House of Federation", and, of course, the New Democratic Party called for the abolition of the other place and proposed that it be replaced by adding 100 members to this House.
On October 25 The Citizen published an interview with Professor John Crispo, an expert in economics, politics, business, journalism and parliamentary procedure, if you accept his word for it. In his new book entitled "Mandate for Canada" Professor Crispo proposes to reform the political process and Parliament. He proposes to do it in much the same way as has been advocated by the New Democratic Party. New members of Parliament would come from party lists made up of candidates selected by their party and elected on the basis of proportional representation. He said that the party-list members would campaign nationally, along with the party leaders, to free them from parochial constituency concerns. He said that this means "you wouldn't have only one Liberal member west of Winnipeg."
In his book Professor Crispo goes on to say that if he were prime minister he would take steps to increase the salaries of federal members to $100,000 per year. I assume that while there may be some things about his book that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre might support, he certainly would not support that proposal.

speechtext: You are absolutely right about that.

speechtext: Professor Crispo went on to say that higher salaries would attract better people, and parliament would become more effective. I would share the view of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that Professor Crispo is not any more accurate in that assessment than he is in any other.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY PARLIAMENTARY REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
In fact I would say that when one considers the various recommendations that had been made to improve the other place, they cannot help but make the Senate look good. Unfortunately, this has led us back to the status quo-to say that the other place does not really need to be reformed because all the proposals of the various political parties seem to have more disadvantages than advantages when subjected to the scrutiny of public opinion.
We need to ask ourselves if there is room, in a democracy, for an appointed upper house. If the answer is yes, then we must address the system of appointment. Many distinguished men and women who have made great contributions in busi-

ness, in the trade unions, in agriculture, education, and the social services, are presently excluded from the political process, primarily because they are not actively partisan.
Let me return to the motion, Mr. Speaker. 1 think motion No. 4 provides hon. members with an opportunity, to pursue the matter when it is referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. The motion deals with the need for redressing the regional imbalance in the House of Commons. That seems to be the essential point of the rationale and the essential basis for the suggested changes.
Two major parties have been referred to, but I would suggest that we now have three national parties in Canada. I consider the New Democratic Party a national party. All three parties are represented in Canada from coast to coast and, in five provinces, all three parties are represented. It is true they are variously weak in different parts of Canada and I appreciate that the motion is intended to redress that imbalance.
There is little argument with the contention that a more balanced representation would lend a more national focus to national party perspectives. I agree it would give the government an improved perspective on the problems and issues in Quebec if we had more representation from that province. As well, it would give the official opposition a better perspective if they had more representation from western Canada.
Not too long ago the Leader of the Opposition went to Calgary and Edmonton to put the cause of his party and his position before audiences there. It is interesting that just after this, The Globe and Mail ran an article with the headline "Trudeau Just Doesn't Get the Message". In the 11 years he was prime minister, the Leader of the Opposition never understood western Canada and that was the main reason for the poor showing of the Liberal party there, the party that once had such a solid hold in the west that it was almost unchallengeable. I speak as one who was born and raised in western Canada, Mr. Speaker. At different times in my life I have lived in the maritimes, British Columbia, Quebec, and now I live in Ontario.
The question is whether the problem of regional imbalance can be addressed by adding 60 or 100 members to the House of Commons, as is proposed by the New Democratic Party. I think the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Baker) touched on some of the logistic problems today. He mentioned the frustration that members of Parliament experience through being unable to put a position forward in the House. Under the proposed solution, more problems might be created than we could ever hope to solve.
Had 60 members been added in the recent federal election on the basis of proportional representation, the breakdown would have been along the following lines: The Liberal party would have 24 more members, the Conservatives would have 22 more members, the New Democratic Party would have 11 more, and the Social Credit party would have three more. I can only point out that had those members been in their places last Tuesday night, the government would have been defeated by a vote of 173 to 165.
November 12, 1979

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY PARLIAMENTARY REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I would interpret that differently. I would say it is one undesirable consequence of this motion.
I think there are other consequences equally undesirable, Mr. Speaker. One is that two classes of members would be created within the House of Commons-one class representing constituencies and the other representing the population at large. One thing that all members of Parliament have in common at present is that they each represent a constituency. We must keep in touch with the grass roots and be responsive to public opinion. There are other reasons as well.
I think there would be an inclination, if the motion were adopted, for the parties to draw their leadership from the lists rather than from those who seek office in a particular constituency. That would be a normal reaction. It would free the leaders of parties from having to campaign within their constituencies, but it would have undesirable consequences. It would made the leadership of the parties less responsive to public opinion. Nothing brings a member of Parliament down to earth more quickly than going back to the constituency and learning what the constituents have to say about what he or she has been doing.
Those at the top of the list would be assured of election and the system would lead to a stagnation of the political elite, as the established party leadership protects its own position at the top and frustrates the political newcomers.
It would encourage the formation of new parties. In my opinion there is no doubt about that, because their leadership would be assured of a seat in the House of Commons if the party obtained even less than 2 per cent of the national vote. This would have the consequence of creating single issue parties. We would see national political parties created across this country that would have as their purpose nothing further than the possible introduction of capital punishment. Another political party might call for the repeal of the abortion lows. Another might call for the repeal of the gun laws. And, heaven forbid, another political party might call for the restitution of prohibition. This conveys to hon. members some of the dreadful consequences of what could happen were the motion eventually followed through and accepted by the government.
Despite the lofty motivation by the mover of this motion, 1 believe that the negative consequences would outweigh the advantages to Canada's political system. We do, however, need a dialogue in the debate on how some of the advantages might be achieved within the context of our present system of direct representation.
In giving my maiden speech in the throne speech debate, I discussed the desirability of introducing changes to the elections act in order to provide for prescribed election dates, that is to say, every four years we would have an election in this country at a time ideally suited to Canada, subject to the government always maintaining the confidence of the House of Commons. In the event it did not and the government fell, and
Parliamentary Representation
a new election was called, we would then return to the four year rotating basis. This would enable all political parties to play the same rules. It would enable candidates in those provinces in which their parties are not normally in favour to be able to get into the field early enough. They would know precisely the date of the next election. They could then work hard to overcome the disadvantages which their national party might have in the particular region. Candidates could organize themselves so as to increase the likelihood of success because of the institution of prescribed election dates.
The last election which resulted in this Thirty-first Parliament was a ghastly experience for many candidates. We were geared up for an election several times. Parties lost some of their best candidates as the result of the prolongation of election periods. The proposals that I have made which I think would have the effect of mitigating some of these circumstances outlined by the mover, would be superior in terms of its consequences.
In conclusion, I commend the mover for putting forward his idea for public debate. I hope he will pursue it in the standing committee. However, 1 would argue that it does not address the real problems of parliamentary representation or effectiveness.
Members of Parliament should enter this chamber through the front door as elected members of constituencies rather than the through the back door because they have been able to get their names on the top of party lists.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY PARLIAMENTARY REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Ottawa-Carle-ton (Mr. Pepin) for presenting this motion designed to allot to each party a number of seats proportionate to the number of votes they get. 1 regret, however, that the Liberal group that had been in power for 16 years did not find time to introduce a bill of that nature. It would certainly have received considerable support in the House.
1 shall be brief, Mr. Speaker. For a few months now the Liberals have been in opposition; they have had time to think things over and now they come with a motion to place democracy at its proper place. Mr. Speaker, it is obvious, as our leader, the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Roy), said on October 11, that the Social Credit party does not have enough members in the House to adequately represent the high percentage of votes received compared to any other party in the House of Commons. And on that matter, 1 think the previous speaker and myself do not have the same figures, because we do not obtain the same results in our calculation. At all events, we will surely have the opportunity to come back to that matter.
The hon. member for Beauce had then taken great care in his remarks on the Speech from the Throne to enlighten us as to the professional representativeness of members. Indeed, an analysis of the outcome of the last general election shows that

November 12, 1979
Parliamentary Representation
a Progressive Conservative member represents 32,000 voters; a Liberal member, 40,000 voters; a New Democrat member, 78,800 voters, and a Social Credit member, 105,000 voters. Mr. Speaker, these figures are from the report of the chief electoral officer. I am not making up anything. 1 am just looking at the results. In light of these figures, comparing the representation of Canadians who voted for the Progressive Conservatives and that of those who voted for the Socreds, we would have 15 members in the House if proportional representation did exist. If we compare ourselves with the Liberals, we should have 13 members in the House. Those are the two oldest parties in the House. They are very much alike and they would be happy if there were no other political group in the House. But I want to tell the House that if there are others, it is because those two have been running the country ever since confederation. Had they been judged satisfactory, there would be no other political party. That is democracy. We should not complain about the fact that some Canadians get together to defend the same principles and express their beliefs in the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, as we can see our struggle for the protection of the rights and privileges of the Social Credit Party of Canada was fully justified. I would like to underline the words of the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) who, last week, as can be seen at page 1054 of Hansard, said, and I quote:
Since the waning political party led by the member for Beauce (Mr. Roy) was not even in a position to run candidates in every Quebec constituency and had no candidate in any other Canadian province-
-while we had fielded 74 candidates out of a possible 76, it was only because of a mishap that we did not run the full 76. But we did have candidates in six Canadian provinces. The hon. member therefore had not verified his facts too closely before saying that we had fielded candidates only in the province of Quebec. As to the "waning" bit, Mr. Speaker, 1 rather like it. As a former farmer for many years, 1 used to watch the beautiful sun setting in the evening, which would encourage me to get up in the morning to make hay. Those who say that our party is waning should not forget that it has met with severe mishaps over the past few years. They should pray the Almighty to protect them against such misfortune. We were forced to get organized at the very last minute and we did the utmost to try to offer the Canadian people some other alternative to the traditional choice. Under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to hurt the feelings of the hon. member for Papineau, but I suggest to him that, when he deals with this issue, he should make comments which are more in line with the facts. I am not asking him to be more charitable, merely to be more just, because justice and charity are two different things. But we have the obligation to practice both virtues.
For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I should like to give another member of the Liberal formation the chance to deal with this motion. Although I want to speak very briefly, 1 want

to say not only that I support the principle of the motion, but that 1 should like this motion to be really considered in a committee, in order to find a way to eliminate the shortcomings of our election system and thereby improve the democratic process in our country. As for me, I am all for democracy, but the real democracy I like to live by daily in the House in our discussions and our relations between Canadians. 1 want that democracy to be really in our minds. We should live by it as perfectly as possible. That is why I support the motion as does my group here in the House, like the Liberal group, and 1 do hope, as was expressed earlier by the group of the New Democratic Party, that we all agree on that and the sooner it comes the better.
Mr. Speaker, if you wonder why I am always speaking in terms of "groups", it is because in his statements in the House the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen) always refers to us as the Social Credit group, whereas we form part of a party, the Social Credit Party of Canada. If they want to speak with different words, I am prepared to go along, but 1 will keep on speaking in terms of "groups" when referring to other political denominations. And 1 do hope that one day the Speaker will have his say and straighten out the record in that respect, for it will be in the best interest of democracy.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY PARLIAMENTARY REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if we were sitting down to design an electoral system for Canada, one of the things we would like to do is work out a system where one candidate in a constituency would get at least 50 per cent of the votes, that whatever combination of individuals or parlies form the government they would have at least 50 per cent of the votes in the country, and that when we come to make decisions in the House of Commons those decisions would be taken by representatives at least representing 50 per cent of the votes in the country. However, what do we have?
We have a system that permits, in a three-way race, a member with as many votes as 33.1 per cent to be elected as representing that region. It has happened. We have a situation in the House of Commons where the government was elected with 36 per cent of the votes cast by Canadians, while Her Majesty's Loyal Official Opposition received 40 per cent of the votes. We have a government coalition made up of the Progressive Conservative Party and the Social Credit party which represents about 41 per cent of the votes cast in the last general election.
To draw the analogy even further and to be honest about it, when we formed the last majority government elected in 1974, we only had between 43 and 44 per cent. I believe there has only been one government in Canada that has been elected with more than a majority of the votes cast, that being the government of the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker in 1958.
When you put on the table what logically ought to happen and what in reality happens, you get a considerable gap. When
November 12, 1979

1 was a backbencher on the government side, it used to worry me that we were the government with 42 to 44 per cent. We did not have a majority in the public at large, but we did have a majority in the House of Commons.
What we have now is a system that, in effect, elects minority governments by popular vote, even though the way those votes are allocated in a purely artificial and historical way results in a majority of seats in the House of Commons. When you examine the situation, you have to agree there there is no logic or rationale to it. Like Topsy, it is something that has "just growed." We have a system that is not satisfactory.
Why is it not satisfactory? 1 will make the argument that it is not satisfactory because it is a system with which the Canadian people are becoming less and less content. That is because the way it operates ensures that their wishes are not represented in the House of Commons. The will that they express in casting their votes is distorted. Therefore, what we have in the House of Commons is a distorted image of what the electorate has actually said.
I want to demonstrate that by using some statistics that are easily accessible. 1 will use a number of years, commening with the year 1968. I will give the percentage of votes for three provinces which I have deliberately selected to show the variations.
In the province of Quebec in 1968, the Liberals received 54 per cent of the vote but 76 per cent of the seats, a tremendous distortion. The Progressive Conservatives had 21 per cent of the vote but only 5 per cent of the seats, an even greater distortion. The NDP received 8 per cent of the vote and no seats. The Social Credit party had 16 per cent of the popular vote and received 19 per cent of the seats, a distortion. In no case was anybody remotely close in terms of their seats with respect to the percentage of votes they received.
I will give the comparable figures for Manitoba. In Manitoba the Liberals received 42 per cent of the votes and 38 per cent of the seats, not a bad fit. The Progressive Conservatives received 31 per cent of the votes but 38 per cent of the seats, a distortion. The NDP was right on, 25 per cent of the votes, 24 per cent of the seats.
Let us look at Alberta. Alberta gave the Liberal party 36 per cent of its votes, and 21 per cent of the seats, under representation. The Progressive Conservatives got 50 per cent of the votes but 79 per cent of the seats, and the NDP received 9 per cent of the votes and no seats.
Let us look at the same figures for 1972. In Quebec the Liberal vote was 49 per cent of the votes and 76 per cent of the seats, a drop of 5 per cent in the popular vote but no difference in the percentage of seats. The Conservatives received 17 per cent of the votes, 3 per cent of the seats; the NDP 6 per cent of the voles and no seats, and the Social Credit 24 per cent of the votes and 21 per cent of the seats.
In Manitoba the figures were more interesting; the Liberals 31 per cent of the votes and 15 per cent of the seats; the Progressive Conservatives 42 per cent of the votes and 62 per cent of the seats, and the NDP, 26 per cent of the votes and 23
Supply
per cent of the seats. In Alberta the Liberal party received 25 per cent of the votes and no seats; the Progressive Conservative party 58 per cent and 100 per cent of the seats; the New Democratic Party 13 per cent of the votes but no seats; and the Social Credit 5 per cent and no seats.
I think the point is clear. If you examine carefully what actually happens in elections, Canadians in Large regions of the country are being discriminated against because their votes do not show up in the political results of those elections. The distortions we have built in totally wreck any kind of valid exchange.
There are about two minutes remaining. The government wants to change private members' hour to allow votes to go through and to allow private members' hour to have an effect. 1 appeal to the government whip and the parliamentary secretary to show their good will by allowing this motion to pass.

speakerposition: Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was in the midst of replying to some pertinent questions which the hon. member for Mada-waska-Victoria had asked. The one I was about to deal with involved an agricultural institution which had been talked about and which has not yet become operative. I have had an opportunity to look into this matter over the supper break to refresh my memory about it, and I will put on record some of the data I learned.
The provincial minister of agriculture has stated his intention to put into place Francophone agricultural training by the fall of 1980. DREE agreed with the province to follow up the recommendation of the provincial agricultural study by considering ways and means of making agricultural training available to Francophones in New Brunswick, and it is my understanding that the provincial government is considering the establishment of a facility in northwest New Brunswick. I believe the province will seek federal assistance from DREE in particular for the purpose of establishing this facility, and when DREE negotiated the current agricultural subsidiary agreement with New Brunswick the possibility of such assistance was contemplated. Should it be requested 1 am certainly ready to consider additional federal aid. As I understand the hon. member's reference to $1 million-
For the airport.

speakerposition: Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext: -I understand there was no specific basis for that proposed educational facility. I also understand that there has been a real problem, as one so often finds in connection with this type of situation, in finding the ideal place for such a facility, and that a former deputy minister of Quebec, Mr. Mercier, was brought in to help evaluate the situation, also, that there was at one point a question as to whether existing institutions might be able to provide that kind of training, which would avoid having to build a school or college for that purpose. However, as I said earlier, I understand the province intends to go ahead with it in northwestern New Brunswick, and my department is very sympathetic toward the idea of assisting in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to thank the minister for his replies. They will shed some light on the matters I inquired about before recess. However, I would like to come back to the issue of the airport and the comment, which he quoted, made by Premier Hatfield when they met a short time after the hon. member became Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. Premier Hatfield implied that he was not in favour of using funds from a federal department concerned mostly with regional economic development for airport facilities or buildings. This is the whole essence of the question, Mr. Chairman. My constituents and myself were told by officials of the air services section, airport facilities, of the
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. McCain).]
federal Department of Transport that it was difficult, if not impossible, to justify the construction of a 6,000-foot runway for jets to link northwestern New Brunswick with the service already provided in Charlo, in the northern part of the province, and in Chatham, in the east. We were told that it was impossible to justify such an allocation of funds, and we were told this by the officials and the advisers of the then minister, the Hon. Otto Lang. We then thought that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion should have a role to play in such situations when other departments do not feel justified in doing the things that need to be done. This should be the basic and the major role of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, namely, to take action when other departments cannot or will not under the law. Otherwise, who needs a Department of Regional Economic Expansion? And what does Premier Hatfield find to say about this when the federal government is paying 100 per cent and 110 per cent of his road building costs as well as legal and engineering fees? He has the gall to tell the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion that his department should not involve itself with airports while we are defraying the entire cost of his roads. This is completely ridiculous! If there is one thing that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion should do, it is to intervene in such cases and to do so vigorously and energetically, Mr. Chairman. I simply can not accept this. 1 respect the minister very much and I know that he wants to promote the development of the region that we represent in the House of Commons. However, I do not accept the arguments attributed to him to the effect that his department should not get involved in such projects. This is quite inaccurate. And 1 implore the minister to re-examine this case, to consider it especially in light of the wants of the local population. I have here a letter sent to Premier Richard Hatfield on May 15, 1979, by his predecessor, the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Les-sard), which says, and 1 quote:
Dear Mr. Hatfield:
I have received your telex of May 9 and your letter of May 8, 1979, concerning the proposed developing regions subagreement.

1 must emphasize at this point that the agreement had not yet been signed and that the point of contention was precisely the funding for the airport project. Minister Lessard goes on to say:

My support for the airport project was based upon the unanimous views of municipal and industrial development groups, that the airport was the number one development priority.
[ Translation]
By what right can a provincial government come by the back door and suggest to the minister that the airport development project is not the number one priority in northwestern
November 12, 1979

New Brunswick, and that a parking facility for a small downtown complex in Edmundston comes before the development of an airport and hence economic development? That is totally beyond me, Mr. Chairman. 1 therefore implore the minister tonight, 1 will not beg him on my knees, but I do urge him to re-examine this case and give justice to the people of northwestern New Brunswick. If the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) wants to change his policy, he will first of all have to come before the House of Commons to tell us that he indeed has the funds necessary to expand the airstrip from its present 4,000 feet to 6,000 feet. But I have news for the Minister of Transport and for the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. MacKay), news which is not very encouraging but which reflects the sorry state in which the eastern provinces find themselves when it comes to getting their share of the pie. We have a regional carrier called Eastern Provincial Airways (1963) Limited. This regional carrier which has held service rights since 1967 for the Atlantic region is interested in acquiring Nordair with other partners and yet the chances of its succeeding in a bid are virtually nil to the extent that when questioning the Eastern Provincial Airways officials at a private meeting, I was told that it is not very likely now that in the foreseeable future their company will be able to provide us with a jet passenger service as is the case for Charlo and Chatham. Worse than that, the company is considering a reduction in the level of services offered to these two other locations. I hope that officials from the Departments of Transport and Regional Economic Expansion will be able to advance arguments to justify building a 6,000-foot runway at a time when the regional carrier is no longer interested in it at least for the next few years to come. There has got to be something going wrong some place, Mr. Chairman, and I will gladly give full credit to the government members who sit across the floor, if we can extend the Saint-Leonard runway to 6,000 feet. I will be the first to congratulate the government for it but what is important is that it must be done without partisan considerations whatsoever. This was the point I wanted to make this evening, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, last week we had a visit from the chiefs representing the bands in the Qu'Appelle Valley area of Saskatchewan who were here to voice serious grievances about the implementation of the DREE agreement respecting the Qu'Appelle Valley. This is an agreement which was, among other things, to straighten out the Qu'Appelle River, control water levels, purify the water system, and improve tourism and recreation opportunities along the Qu'Appelle River. This agreement-and I am trying to reach the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion in bringing up these grievances-affects eight Indian bands representing 6,000 registered Indians and 176,000 acres of Indian land.
The difficulty is this: the authority administering this DREE agreement in Saskatchewan on the Qu'Appelle River has been operating with little consultation with these Indian bands. The

Indians get very short notice one day that parts of their lands are to be flooded and that they must remove their cattle from the land so that work can take place, and because of this what I would call very blatant disregard of individuals and peoples who are along the territory subject to the DREE agreement, they came to Ottawa to voice their grievances.
They told me that they tried to see the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion to explain to him how they were being treated by officers of both the Saskatchewan government and the federal government who administer this agreement, but that the minister could not or would not see them. I hear that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development saw them, but not the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. If he has seen them, that is well and good, but I hear that he did not at that particular time. If he did, what I was shocked by was not that the minister treated the Indians this way, but that the officials who implement and administer this agreement would have so little consideration for such a large group of people who have such important rights in the riparian lands along the Qu'Appelle River. What can the minister do, or what does he intend to do to make these officials more accountable to him, one of the political authorities in this agreement?
I see that the agreement is a $44 million agreement. Of that from the minister's department is a contribution of $18 million, and there are other moneys contributed by other departments of the federal government. However, the minister's department is the principal department. I would like to know what might be done by our Minister of Regional Economic Expansion to make these officials more accountable to his authority and perhaps to an authority in Saskatchewan. Further, will the minister instruct these officials to take a more enlightened approach to consultation with these eight bands, the 6,000 registered Indians in that area? Knowing the minister's approach to these matters, I am sure that if he knows about these things he would try to correct them. I would like to hear his response to these particular problems.

Mr. Chairman, first I would like to congratulate the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. MacKay) who is also responsible for the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Tonight I shall dwell on the activities of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and I will tackle the question of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation constructing homes for elderly people when we study Bill C-20 which, although sponsored by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie), is indirectly related to the activities of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion.
Mr. Chairman, the report published by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion at the beginning of 1977 stressed the critical state of the economy in the province of Quebec, especially in greater Montreal. Following this study, the department had decided to create a special zone in Montreal to develop the economy, to develop the industry with a view to creating jobs in Montreal itself as well as in the metropolitan region.
Mr. Chairman, that agreement signed in July, 1977, covered a period of three years due to end soon. 1 would like to know from the minister what the intentions of the government are. Does it intend to continue to consider Montreal and its suburbs as a special area as a result of the many requests that have already been made by members from that area, which were also endorsed by the Montreal Chamber of Commerce at its annual meeting? Then I think it would be important that the minister say to the House how he intends to continue this program and whether he intends to amend the grant structure and selection standards.
Mr. Chairman, after two years of operation the grants that were distributed or handed out by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion totalled $47 million, which means a total investment of $275 million in the metropolitan area. But because of circumstances that might not have facilitated investment in Quebec, particularly in the Montreal area, the anticipated success was cut by nearly half, and it seemed to me that the requirements for approval of the projects that were submitted were such that we had to eliminate quite a number of industries which might have qualified, which might have contributed to the economic sector. But because of overly stringent selection standards several of these projects had to be turned down. 1 know that in the area I represent, Ville-de-Lav-al, several industrialists wanted to take advantage of this federal program of assistance to industry, but precisely because of the standards, they were unable to qualify for a grant. So I would ask the minister whether he intends to recognize the Montreal area as a special area, how much the grants would be, does he intend to increase those amounts, and what will be the selection standards for industries to qualify for those grants?

My second comment, Mr. Chairman-and I believe this is rather important in the present context-is that we received requests from certain industrialists who have already had their programs approved but who, while carrying out their projects, had to change the design or structural plans with a resulting increase in the total investment cost.
In view of the changes made in carrying out the construction, would the minister consider increasing or extending the amount of the grant which was about 15 per cent on investments, considering the projected addition as a result of those changes and adding the 15 per cent grant to the one already approved? My last remark, Mr. Chairman, is that the public is very much concerned about a project which was the subject of numerous representations in this House and in several departments, and which was discussed at the meeting of Canadian government ministers with ministers from the government of Quebec. And that is where my comments echo those of my colleague from the "Republic of Madawaska" who stated that the government should also have power to take initiatives when it comes to accepting huge amounts of federal government funds in provincial government projects.
We had a project which had been approved, a contribution from the Canadian government through the Department of Regional Economic Expansion for extending highway 13A between Mirabel and Montreal, which should encourage the development of cargo in Mirabel. And we are waiting, Mr. Chairman. These funds have been approved, have been deposited for the benefit of the province of Quebec, and they have been there for two years. We do not know what will happen. We heard this money would be used for improving commuter trains in Montreal, and yet this was not the original purpose of these funds which had been approved by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion for extending highway 13A. It amounted to $30 million. So, Mr. Chairman, I wish to know if the minister will wield his power of initiative in his meetings with provincial governments so that these priorities also reflect the priorities of those who made the application and not necessarily the priorities of a province. 1 also express my disappointment concerning the meeting of federal ministers. The Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. La Salle), who is here tonight, took part in that meeting where they discussed the priorities about the famous package of almost $100 million set aside for establishing the General Motors plant in the province of Quebec.
That amount was available for the Department of Regional Economic Expansion under the previous government and we urged that these funds be used to reduce the deficit at Mirabel international airport through the improvement of a rapid transit system between Montreal and Mirabel aimed at giving better ground service to passengers. If we cannot improve the service, the airlines will choose to land in Toronto or elsewhere. Because of that, the deficit is always increasing at Mirabel international airport. And I remember perfectly that
November 12, 1979

some members of the opposition questioned the deficit at Mirabel when we had the possibility to use that amount of almost $100 million set aside for the General Motors plant. You know what the result was.
I had asked the then minister of supply and services in this House if he considered as a priority the improvement of the rapid transit system between Montreal and Mirabel. The minister said that he would follow the priorities of the Quebec government. I had much reservation at the time of the adjournment when I mentioned my concern about the attitude of the ministers of the Parti Quebecois government who never showed any interest in the development of Mirabel international airport, as they always said that it was a federal project and that it was up to the Canadian government to improve its ground transportation system between Montreal and Mirabel to reduce the deficit which is increasing every year.
Mr. Chairman, 1 conclude by asking the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion to use his power of initiative to study the development of the Montreal area and to discuss with his colleagues of the Department of Transport and the Department of Supply and Services not only the use of the $30 million for the extension of highway I3A but also the construction of a ground transportation system between Mirabel and Montreal.

Mr. Chairman, if I can deal with some of the important questions the hon. member for Laval raised, first of all he is quite right in saying that there has been a substantial benefit to the Montreal area by virtue of the agreement signed on July I, 1977. As the hon. member and his colleagues well know, it has been suggested that the area be expanded to include three additional counties. 1 believe they are Vaudreuil, Soulange, and Huntington. Also it has been suggested that the criteria be changed in order to facilitate a more flexible approach. At the present time the categories which are eligible, just to put them on the record, are industries dealing in prepared and quick frozen food, metal fabricating, machinery, transportation equipment, electrical products, chemicals and chemical products, scientific and professional equipment, sporting goods and toys, which tend to be rather compartmentalized. Also he knows that the present criteria for the Montreal special area is for projects with a minimum investment of $100,000, that it is for capital costs, and that no other allowance is made.
I do not want to get into too great detail at the present time, because I know the hon. member will understand it would not be proper at a time when this very important subject is before the economic development committee of our cabinet. It

speakerposition: Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext: The matter of improving the transportation links to Mirabel is something about which my colleague, the Minister of Transport, and I had some important discussions. Also we discussed the matter with the Minister of Supply and Services. It is a question of consultation as well with the city of Montreal, as the hon. member well knows, because a project of this nature must have a very broad understanding and co-operation from all levels of government. It is very much on our minds. We have not forgotten the necessity of improving the transportation links to Mirabel. Despite the criticism of that airport, that it is incurring substantial deficits and so on, the fact is that it is there. We must exercise the responsibility we have to improve its utilization. I can assure the hon. member that we are looking at that.

speakerposition: Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext:
I am not so certain I recall with precision the other questions which the member asked, but I want to say to him, and in partial response to the hon. member for Madawas-ka-Victoria, that one of the things we hope to do under our cabinet structure is to try to get a greater degree of co-operation from the line departments. It is quite true, if the line departments were exercising a great ambition in recognizing all aspects of regional development, that there would not be that great need for DREE. However, now that we have this department which, as the hon. member knows, was created about ten years ago, the challenge is to make certain that the line departments do not forget their own particular interest simply because DREE is there.
1 realize it is a fine line, but we must do the best we can to maximize the kind of co-ordinated approach which will give us great leverage and expand the budgetary prowess of DREE by enlisting the resources of other departments. I am sure that is what the premier of New Brunswick had in mind. As I mentioned before, I can assure the member that a similar airstrip was completed in the Port Hawkesbury area of Nova Scotia.
These types of airstrips, if they are to be useful, and if they are to justify the money spent on them, must be utilized for the type of air carrier service to connect some of the points he has

November 12, 1979
