mentioned, and indeed some of the points in Nova Scotia, with a low cost, frequent, and convenient air service which will help us in the entire maritime regions. The hon. member can be assured that 1 am interested in getting that airport built. Whether we do it with funds from the airport development fund through the Department of Transport, whether we do it from DREE funds, or whether we can persuade the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce or some other department to help us, the important thing is to develop the airport. I share his dedication in that respect.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word or two about DREE also. One item which irked me no end when 1 was in the provincial government, and which I believe irks other provincial governments, is the fact that DREE is applicable only in certain areas within a province. It does not matter whether the raw materials are there, whether there is housing there or the other necessities to make that industry successful; it has to be done within the boundaries of that particular area.
A year ago a matter was brought to the attention of the then minister in charge of DREE. He was sympathetic to a project in the Drumheller area where there was a need for the repair of oil well equipment. The expertise was there in the form of a farm machine company which had been selling and repairing farm machines for years. The factory was there, the old Prowler plant which had been left vacant for several years. Everything seemed to be there to make a successful and highly profitable operation, except the capital that was required. To borrow $500,000 at 13 per cent or 14 per cent made the item prohibitive. Approximately 16 to 30 people would have been employed in that particular area.
I would suggest to the minister if economic expansion is going to be real in this country, that it should be done where there is a need for that expansion; not applied to a certain part of a province only. This was only applicable in northern Alberta. There are several places. Southern Alberta had the opportunity of employing several men and women, many of whom came from other provinces in Canada. It was denied because it did not happen to be sitting in the right location. I suggest to the hon. minister that the economic expansion division should deal with expansion wherever and whenever, and particularly wherever the opportunity presents itself, and not be made applicable only to certain areas within each province.

speakerposition: Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will take the representations of the hon. member for Bow River very seriously. But I should like to point out to him and the House that it is the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. If we accede to the constant requests for expanding into other territories and making it a uniform program across the country, as laudable as that may be, we will have to take the "Regional" out and just call it the department of economic expansion, which has a certain appeal. Since it is geared at this particular point in time to provide the maximum amount of aid where it is most needed and where certain provinces have more resources than others, then I think we must be very careful in expanding the

territory to make this possible until we have the budgetary resources to do it. But I will certainly take that representation and have my officials study it.

Mr. Chairman, I have been talking with the minister since the House opened, but I want to take this opportunity to congratulate him officially on his new job. All members here from Nova Scotia and, indeed, all Atlantic members, regardless of their party affiliations, are looking forward to the minister giving the leadership that is so badly needed at this time in Canada's history.
I do not think anyone at this time should be prepared, after a ten-year period, to wipe out the Department of Regional Economic Expansion until we are damned sure that we have something better with which to replace it. During the committee work I have done, along with the minister, during the last four or five years I have naturally been interested in my own area which is one of the hardest economically hit areas of the country. We have always tried during this work to keep in mind the larger picture and how we might improve the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. I hope that under this minister we can give consideration to the ideas he brought to the committee as a member of it while in the official opposition.
I know that the minister is a good listener, and that he realizes there is not one definite theory regarding regional development, but rather a whole melange that has been brought from western Europe and incorporated into various aspects of the development of the institutions which we have experienced, all the way from the area development agency through to the Atlantic Development Board, and now the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
Regional development needs to be improved, and we will all be making our contributions having regard to new ideas that have been and are coming in the field of theoretical and applied development. In this way we will try to make this important department of government even better, at a time when the nation is obviously suffering great economic constraint, just as are many countries in the western world. This country is going to go through the wringer, it appears to me, to a very much greater extent than some other countries. We will need this department because those areas that suffer most from national monetary and fiscal policies are the poorer areas, including the Atlantic provinces. These are the areas that always suffer most from the application of fiscal and monetary policies designed for the central provinces and the richer provinces such as Alberta.
I am talking about the application of tight monetary policies in the fight against inflation, for example, when combined with fiscal restraints that are very severe. The Atlantic provinces have always suffered and will continue to suffer from the application of such policies unless and until the Department of Regional Economic Expansion receives help in co-ordinating the efforts by all departments involved.
November 12, 1979

I agree with the minister that even if the funding that is provided is increased, and it must be increased even in a period of restraint if the emphasis is to be on helping the poorer regions, there has to be greater co-ordination, along the lines he talked about, between certain departments, whether they be transportation, supply and services, or public works. This must be the case in order that we will have in this country a sort of new co-ordinating institution, and it will naturally involve provincial input. If we obtain that co-ordination we will be going a long way toward using the funds allocated to DREE and other institutions for the maximum benefit of those regions that require this development assistance.
These efforts should be made at a first stage in this type of co-ordinating committee. We would then see better returns for our bucks, which seems to be the obsession of the department of the treasury at this time. We do not need a great many cutbacks in order to do this type of job. What we need are more efficient spending and better uses of the money through co-ordination.
Since we have the Department of Regional Economic Expansion it seems to me that this co-ordination should be done by that department, particularly in areas such as parts of Quebec and the Atlantic region, just to mention two. This co-ordination must be done through the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. Unless and until the Prime Minister and the rest of the cabinet bring themselves to this conviction, we will not see the greatest benefits. The Prime Minister and his cabinet must realize that there is only one way to help the Atlantic region and that is by not only making the necessary bucks available in order to improve the earned per capita income rather than just the per capita income, but by coordinating the spending of those funds.
We want jobs. We want creative jobs. We want ten-year plans. If that sounds socialistic or communistic, I do not care. We must have this if we are going to re-establish the balance in this country.
It is kind of ironic that Ontario is getting worried now because of price increases. I do not make light of that, but we in the Atlantic provinces have been suffering and have had this grievance for many, many years, as many of us have pointed out in the House. We who come here from whatever walk of life know what the game is here before us. We know about the small population we have in the Atlantic provinces. We know we do not have very much clout, and many times we have to go begging for the crumbs that come from the central provinces, and now from a rich province like Alberta.

REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON FIRST MINISTERS' MEETING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps at the beginning 1 might have the permission of the House to lay on the table two copies of "An Outline of Proposed Initial Stage of National Energy Strategy," a background paper that was published earlier today in both official languages.

speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON FIRST MINISTERS' MEETING
speechtext:
I would like to take the opportunity to express my apology to opposition spokesmen on the other side in that it was only recently that we were able to get a copy of my statement to them. This had to do with the relatively short time between the conclusion of our discussions and my desire to come and report as directly as possible to the House of Commons. I want also to indicate, sir, how much I appreciate the courtesy of members on both sides in providing unanimous consent so that I might report to Parliament on my meeting today with other first ministers.
As hon. members know, today's discussion centred on the proposals put forth by this government to achieve our goal of making Canada self-sufficient in energy by 1990. Those proposals previously had been the subject of extensive consultation between Ottawa and the provinces, and 1 believe the positive tone of discussions today reflected the value of frank

November 12, 1979
Energy
and extensive consultation in a federal system. Sir, that is a pattern we intend to continue.
I am pleased, for our country, to be able to report substantial agreement among first ministers on the major outlines of a comprehensive energy policy for Canada. The first ministers unanimously endorsed our central goal of energy self-sufficiency. We agreed it is dangerous to the economic future of our country to ignore a situation where so many Canadians, especially in Quebec and in Atlantic Canada, are dependent on unreliable foreign oil supplies.
The important element of price remains to be negotiated. As 1 told the conference, that is, jurisdictionally, a decision for the producing provinces and the national government, but we wanted to take the pricing decision only after we had the opportunity to hear from other parts of Canada, and know how price increases would affect those regions. I was impressed by the realism of first ministers in recognizing that, while price increases are never easy, the consequences of failing to act would be much more serious for Canada. They would expose us to supply interruptions which could devastate the economy of Canada and could leave Canada relying upon unstable foreign sources of oil-sources which simply cannot be counted on. Against that background we will be meeting representatives of the producing provinces this week to seek a pricing regime for oil and natural gas, designed to increase Canada's ability to supply our own oil and gas, to encourage conservation, and to encourage substitution of alternate fuels.
Sir, today we proposed a special tax on incremental oil company profits to help finance Canadian energy development. Officials of our government will be consulting with provinces and the industry to design the most effective tax.
We proposed a Canadian energy bank to help Canadians invest in long term and essential Canadian energy projects. Several provinces, 1 am pleased to report, have agreed to take a look at contributing equity financing to that bank. The federal government itself expects to contribute about $1.5 billion to equity, over the next four years, to help build Canada's energy potential.
Officials will also meet to identify conservation projects where work can begin immediately. I indicated our intention to propose a co-operative program to help individuals retrofit oil-burning furnaces. We would be prepared to contribute to an industrial energy conservation program in Atlantic Canada. Regarding home insulation, several provinces have indicated that local needs would be better served if the Canadian Home Insulation Program, CHIP, were under provincial control, and we are prepared to work out arrangements under which CHIP would be transferred, together with increased federal funding. [Translation]
First ministers strongly supported the need for new initiatives to encourage increased substitution of more plentiful energy sources for oil. Particular attention was given to the opportunity for expanded natural gas markets in Ontario, Quebec and perhaps the maritime provinces, but there was also recognition of the other sources available in particular

regions, for example, greater use of wood waste in British Columbia, increased coal production in Nova Scotia, further hydro development in Manitoba, Quebec and Newfoundland, and expanded development of renewable energy sources across the country. Officials of federal and provincial governments are beginning work immediately to identify areas where substitution can start in 1980.

We have also discussed with first ministers means to help Canadians who will be least able to deal with price increases, and to deal with other specific problems. Those measures will be dealt with either in the federal budget, or in connection with the next first ministers' conference which has been rescheduled for December 17 and 18. That change in date will allow officials to conclude the work flowing from today's conference, and will allow first ministers to also deal with other matters.
[ Translation]
Leaders of 11 governments met to discuss a complex and difficult subject on which there are some legitimate differences of view. Those differences were aired honestly and openly- but without acrimony and within an over-all spirit of partnership. 1 want to express my appreciation publicly of the positive spirit in which provincial premiers came together.

As 1 said at the conference, Mr. Speaker, Canadians have a choice. We can ignore realities, or we can face them.
We have before us the opportunity to provide Canadian industry with a permanent cost advantage over American competitors. We have before us the opportunity to ensure all Canadians reliable and secure energy supplies "made in Canada." We have before us the opportunity to launch a major new era of energy development and a major new commitment to energy conservation in which all Canadians can share.
On the basis of today's discussions, Mr. Speaker, 1 believe Canadians have every reason for confidence that their governments will choose to seize the energy opportunity that is ours.
We have further discussions to continue; we have further negotiations ahead of us, but 1 wanted to come directly from the conference to report to the House of Commons upon the progress that was realized today.

The cost to the Canadian consumers of the present government's plan has been estimated by the government of Ontario, not by us but by another Conservative government, in 1980 to be $5.4 billion. That is going to be the cost of that so-called policy. Under the federal excise tax alone that the government is planning, the federal government would get $2.8 billion. If you estimate the cost of the so-called policy, it is equivalent in 1980 to a 33 per cent increase in personal income tax to Canadian citizens.

The Prime Minister likes to make much of the so-called new spirit of federal-provincial co-operation. We have never seen a debate as acrimonious as the one we have seen in the last few months on this particular energy question

among the provinces, particularly between the province of Ontario and the province of Alberta.
In case the Prime Minister feels I would not be representing history properly, I would like to quote a statement that Premier Lougheed made on August 15, 1979, at Conference-La Malbaie. At page 2 of his statement he said this:
After the dispute between the federal and Alberta governments in 1973 over the federal oil export tax and other matters, the government of Canada and the government of Alberta over the next few years worked out arrangements with regard to pricing and development of energy supply that were clearly in the best interests of all Canada.
That came from the prime minister of Alberta. Tonight we are being told that there was useful discussion-everybody was for motherhood, including self-sufficiency-but on price there is no agreement. On excise tax there was no agreement this morning, and the Prime Minister certainly did not report any agreement tonight. The Prime Minister enunciated four objectives this morning for his policy. Frankly, one should not quarrel with those objectives. First, that the price of oil must be high enough to bring on new sources of supply and the price regime must provide industry enough certainty to plan ahead. Second, we must encourage more effective conservation. Third, we must accelerate the substitution of cheaper and more plentiful fuels and reduce our use of oil. Fourth, we must increase the proportion of Canadian ownership in the Canadian energy industry. That is great. Frankly, it is a mere repetition of what was in the white paper that we issued in 1976. There are a few things missing, because I could suggest that you read the white paper at page 126. What we proposed as objectives were:

Certainly we would be more understanding of the situation in which the government finds itself if the government had created the energy supplies allocation board that we have urged them to create for months, which they have not yet created in spite of our regular pleas to proceed with it.

What are we going to do? According to the government we are going to increase the oil price in Canada to something like 90 per cent of the Chicago composite price. It is a very complex phrase that will probably fool a few Canadians-I hope not-but, in effect, what is being said is that we will reach or at least come very close to international prices. What is the Chicago composite price? According to the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources figures the Chicago price in November, 1979, was $23.71 a barrel. This compares to an international price of $25.68 and a Canadian price, in Toronto, of $15.63. Because of U.S. policy which will completely deregulate U.S. oil prices in the next few years, the Chicago price will be $43.46 in 1985.
I hear an hon. member laugh over there. It is not going to be so funny for Canadians when they have to pay that kind of price in five years' time.

At that time, if the government has its way, Canadians will be paying $41.29 or slightly below, which is about 260 per cent higher than we are paying today. In effect it is estimated that the Chicago price will be higher than the international price if current predictions forecasted are maintained as to what will happen to the international price. This is the type of "pig in a poke" that this government is trying to get us to buy. Not only do we say that it is not necessary for Canada to go to international prices, we say it is a wrong policy for this country.
The government likes to refer to the white paper of 1976 when the world price was $11.50. Again, I remind the government that we stated at that time:
It is the federal government's objective to see domestic oil prices increase to a level sufficient to bring on new Canadian supplies. To the degree that this level is lower than international oil prices, it is a differential for the benefit of Canadian consumers and Canadian producers, industrial and agricultural.
What is meant is that we should have a price that is determined in Canada for Canadians and on the basis of Canadian costs, not on the basis of the cartel price, which is the OPEC price, by whatever name you want to call it. We agree with the government of Ontario that the target for the Canadian price should be the cost of producing Canadian oil and gas, not the price determined abroad on a completely artificial basis, a basis that has no relationship to what it actually costs to produce Canadian oil and gas.
The second point is that we disagree with the way the government is going in trying to reach its goal.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to suggest to the Prime Minister and to this government that we disagree not only with their objective but with the way they have chosen to achieve it. Increasing prices at this point at such a rapid and excessive rate is totally inappropriate, in our view. The impact on the cost of living and Canada's economic growth will be highly negative. In this period of record interest rates, we maintain this is no time for the oil price increases envisaged by the government.
Even the Ontario government is looking at a resulting 137,000 lost jobs if the government proposal is implemented. Those figures are frightening. They are equivalent to closing down or laying off whole cities likes Calgary, Hamilton, Quebec, or again Halifax and St. John's together. Under our regional circumstances, such a policy is indefensible.
There would be a number of other aspects on which we would like to question the government. We will have an
[Mr. Lalonde.)
November 12, 1979

opportunity to do so tomorrow when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) is in Committee of the Whole to answer on his estimates. We will be taking this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to question the minister and try to get more complete information on the government proposal and its implications.
There is reference to regional disparities, but the government decided not to deal with or eliminate these regional disparities. It chose to charge everyone the world price, by increasing oil prices at the same rate for everybody. Everyone recognizes the need for increased conservation and the substitution and development of alternate sources of energy. But we disagree with this government when they show intellectual and moral bankruptcy by simply relying on market forces to attain such objectives. If only they were to implement the proposals introduced by the government in February on conservation and alternate sources of energy, there would be no need for the astronomical price increases they are now proposing.

subtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON FIRST MINISTERS' MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by saying that the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) need not apologize for the delay in sending an advance statement to opposition spokespersons. Given the exigencies of the day, I quite understand that he was not able to produce that in time.
I want to say that at the outset. There was simply no possibility. I want to make it clear on behalf of our party that time was a consideration, and we accept that reality. Having said that, I am not going to agree with much else that I find in the Prime Minister's statement or in that marvellous exposition we just heard from the party to my right. They are at it again. I will be very brief on that point.
The energy critic for the Liberal party has once again managed to convey to the House that they are consistent on one point, that is, they can consistently reverse themselves on every important question that comes before the people of Canada. Just a year ago this month, the then Liberal minister said, "Our policy has been and still is to move crude oil prices at the wellhead toward world levels". That was when the Liberals were on the government side. They are now concerned about interest rates, again an interesting reversal. I will leave the Liberals to the hypocrisy in which they have deeply embedded themselves, and the people of Canada have well perceived that reality.
I want to come to a matter of substance on the government side and clearly indicate that there is a major disagreement in this House and in this country about the direction in which the government is taking us. The Prime Minister indicated that the one thing on which there was no agreement was the matter of price. As everyone knows, if that is not the total issue, it certainly constitutes 90 per cent of the issue.
It is not merely platitudinous to say everyone agrees that something has to be done about conservation. Everyone agrees we should be moving toward self-sufficiency in our energy production, if we can do it. I am among those, along with the government and people in the Liberal party, who say we can
Energy
do it if we have the right programs in this country. In that respect we are very fortunate compared to many others, so there is no debate about those matters.
The real debate in this country, and it is a fundamental one that goes to the root of our prospects as an industrial nation right now, is concern about the matter of price. The Prime Minister said there was no agreement on that. I am not exactly surprised, to understate it a bit, that there was no agreement. The Prime Minister repeated in his brief statement tonight the fundamental argument the government has relied on for justifying an upward movement in price.
The fundamental argument repeated by the Prime Minister tonight is that we need it to have higher revenues to make the investment that is required to bring more energy resources on stream. If an argument could be made for that, if it were essential that we had upward mobility in prices of the kind the Prime Minister talked about to achieve that end, then one has to take it very seriously. Speaking for my colleagues, I say we would. However, I say to the Prime Minister that, frankly, the evidence is not in for that, nor has he provided it. It is simply a bald assertion.
I want to quote from a document produced a week ago by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn). I quote from the footnote on page 15:
Figure 3-
That is of the table in this document.
-indicates that the accrual to industry-
That is the oil industry.
-in the continuation of existing policy-
That is without any upward movement.
-is sufficient to cover an aggressive expenditure pattern throughout the 1980s.
In other words, with the existing pricing arrangement there is sufficient revenue there, and I would add if we pay attention to what we could be doing in this country with Petro-Canada, to get the exploration that the people of Canada need without additional increases. 1 ask the Prime Minister to pay a little more attention to the document produced by one of his minister's departments.
Second, and this is why I proposed in all seriousness on behalf of my party a couple of weeks ago the suggestion for a commission on prices and profits in the oil industry, and this is one of the things I emphasized, it is essential in this country to get an independent body that looks at pricing and profit decision-making in the context of what may be needed to bring further resources on stream.
Such a body is necessary if we are to make an objective analysis which could be presented to the opposition, to the government, and to the people of Canada, of how much was really needed, particularly, but by no means exclusively, when we have a firm like Petro-Canada, publicly owned and controlled, already in existence. The government turned it down. I repeat, we strongly need such a commission which could show

November 12, 1979
Energy
us whether we should take at face value the rhetoric of the oil companies. But 1 can say, on the basis of figures which have come in, on the basis of the document produced by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, that it is certainly our conclusion that the exorbitant profits made by the oil companies already do not entitle them to get any revenue additional to that already committed by the government. That is the evidence. If a contrary case is to be made, surely we need new evidence to support it. The government has not provided such evidence at all.
Now 1 turn to the nub of the problem. Moving prices upward in this country at the speed the government has in mind, creates a twofold problem. First, as the government knows, it hits every consumer; it hits fishermen on the east coast, it hits farmers on the prairies who have to drive tractors, it hits every consumer in Ontario and British Columbia very seriously indeed. No one disputes this. The cost of living will go right out of sight in this country in the next couple of years if we proceed with this plan.
I want, now, to shift to the industrial argument. The Prime Minister went to Tokyo last summer. I will say one thing: I think it was a fit of midsummer madness that led the Government of Canada to agree at that conference in Tokyo with other industrial countries to go to world price levels. It is not accidental. To whose advantage was it? 1 will tell you, Mr. Speaker. It was to Japan's advantage, it was to Germany's advantage, to France's advantage, to the United States' advantage. All those countries are either totally or almost totally dependent on imported oil. They do not have access, as we have in the future, to becoming self-sufficient. But they were well aware that Canada was at last beginning to compete in the industrial world, that we had in certain sectors developed a potential, at least, to cut into their markets. So it was to their advantage to convince the Canadian Prime Minister that one of the industrial nations at Tokyo, the only one there that had energy supplies, should move oil prices up to world levels. That takes away from Canadian industry a competitive advantage. I can only say that it is a disastrous course of action for this country to take. I want to place this in a serious context of national unity.
One way of looking at this country, though by no means the only way, is to see it as a regional bargain. We have the Crow rate for western Canadians. 1 said in Prince Albert just ten days ago, as a man from Ontario, that we support the Crow rate which enables Canadian farmers to ship their grain for about one quarter of the amount it costs American farmers. That subsidy for Canadian farmers in the west is justifiable and we will defend it; we don't fool around talking about getting rid of it, like some members of the Prime Minister's party have been doing publicly.
Similarly, we have provided preferential freight rates to certain areas of Atlantic Canada under DREE, and special programs, programs we would like to see expanded and developed. But we have said, also, that in the industrial heartland, which happens to be mainly in Ontario, there has been a traditional national policy, built, in part, on tariffs, to ensure

industrial development for Ontario and also for Quebec. 1 say to the Prime Minister that this bargain has to be maintained. Right now we are embarking on a course which could completely destroy the competitive advantage of industry in our industrial heartland.
1 say this; if Ontario were ten provinces, if we had smaller provinces like the Americans have states, we would be likely to see it as a region and maybe we would not witness the ganging up psychologically which seems to be taking place, in my view, in many parts of the country.
Does the Prime Minister really think the Germans in the south of Germany would embark upon a course of action which threatened the Ruhr Valley? Would the Japanese in rural areas outside of Yokohama embark upon a course of action which threatened the whole industrial base of Japan? Would the Americans in the south or the west embark on a course of action which would threaten their industrial empire which is in the northeast of the United States? To ask the question is to answer it. The Japanese would not do it; the Germans would not do it; the Americans would not do it. I am saying that Canadians ought not to do it to the province of Ontario because it would damage our whole country, and very seriously.

subtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON FIRST MINISTERS' MEETING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON FIRST MINISTERS' MEETING
speechtext:
1 appeal to the Prime Minister, who says he has not reached a decision on price, to think about this very seriously. There is no good reason, in my mind, for raising the price of gas and oil at all at this point. There is no good argument in its favour as far as 1 can see. There is an argument that favours certain regions. Of course, if I were looking at the question from a short-range perspective, from British Columbia, say, and 1 had some gas reserves, I might say "Yes, this is advantageous to me", or if 1 were in Saskatchewan, I would be inclined to say, "Yes, an upward movement would be favourable." It is understandable. Premiers from those areas cannot be expected to be something other than provincial premiers, and 1 do not say that in any critical sense.
But 1 say to the Prime Minister that he has a responsibility to the nation as a whole, and that the nation as a whole requires a low cost energy policy so that Canadian industry can get moving-and we need to get Canadian industry moving because we need jobs for Canadians. With more than a million unemployed, in real numbers, this gives us a chance. It is a chance the Germans would seize upon; it is a chance the Japanese would seize upon; it is a chance the Americans would seize upon. It is time we came to our senses as an industrial nation and seized upon it as well, and kept those prices down.

We want to look into the possibility of using wood and other sources of energy. We feel that is really imperative in this country because we not only need new sources of oil but we also have to learn to make better use of what other sources are available.

Mr. Speaker, I do not understand that. 1 think it is a startling enunciation of policy by the Prime Minister. I think that, as established in the House, we cannot discuss new taxing policies with individuals who are involved with it. The tradition of this Parliament has been for the government to do the research, to make proposals, to have them debated and passed, but not to discuss them with the companies beforehand. Anyway, Mr. Speaker, we will debate this later on.
However, I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether he knows of any producing country in the world today which is charging to its own consumers the international price for its oil. 1 have been to Saudi Arabia, Iran, Ecuador, Venezuela, and I have found that the price they charge their citizens is not the international price at all. This is the price they charge their customers abroad, but not their own citizens.

subtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON FIRST MINISTERS' MEETING
speechtext:
Let me deal with both those matters. First of all, we want to be sure that we have the best possible tax. We think that one of the problems with the taxing practice in the past has been that taxes have been designed all too often by people who did not understand their impact. We want to be sure we know what this tax is doing, and that is why we will be calling upon the widest possible range of advice. I say that if there are members opposite-and there is the former parliamentary secretary to the minister of finance, the former minister of finance, and a former tax lawyer who have proposals to make-we would certainly welcome their advice as to the effectiveness of the tax.
On the other matter, we are not proposing to raise Canadian prices to international levels. What we are proposing is to end a situation where Canadadian consumers are left at the mercy of decisions that are taken by oil suppliers in unstable lands.

Mr. Chairman, before the Prime Minister came to the House with his statement on the agreement that has been reached at the premiers' meeting today and on the oil situation, I had mentioned a couple of suggestions to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion which he might adopt in order to improve the department. Since the time is getting on, I would like to concentrate-in view of something the Prime Minister has said, and although we will be getting into it in more detail tomorrow with the Minister of DREE- on something that is desperately important to our areas. I would like to underline the word "desperately" at this time.
I have here the following telegram which was sent to the minister on November 8 by the president of District 26 United Mine Workers of America, William H. Marsh. It reads as follows:
Almost daily increases by Arabs in oil prices increasing energy prices and power prices in Canada and particularly in Nova Scotia. Federal oil subsidies to Nova Scotia rising above $70 million. Consider immediate action on opening of new mine in Donkin Morien area imperative. Please act as quickly as possible.
The Halifax Chronicle-Herald considered this to be so important that in their front page editorial of their November 5 issue there is a column entitled, "Energy sufficiency: shy on performance". In spite of what we have been told by the Prime Minister tonight regarding what came out of the meeting this afternoon, that title still holds for the whole of Canada. The editorial relates to the situation in Nova Scotia about which most of you know. We are, next to Prince Edward Island, importers of the largest amounts of foreign oil of any province in this country. In tune with the title of the editorial, we in Canada have energy sufficiency but are shy on performance. The editorial reads in part:
Our best bet, say the experts, is to dig coal and convert our generating stations to thermal generation. But we are witnessing a frustrating display of foot-dragging and lack of motivation in the development of the mines needed to produce the coal.
We have plans-by the dozen. We have promises-by the hundreds. But we're shy on performance.
How many times have we been told that federal funds are forthcoming for the development of mines at Donkin? The rehabilitation of existing collieries in Cape Breton? The enlargement of coal-fired power development at Lingan? The coal exploration program to measure the potential of the coal reserves on Cape Breton Island and on the mainland of Nova Scotia?

November 12, 1979
Supply
In order to keep the Donkin mine project from falling so far behind, the provincial government has had to make the unusual step of advancing funds to a federal agency-
And it is an unusual step in relations between the federal and provincial governments. It goes on to read:
-the Cape Breton Development Corporation-on the understanding Ottawa will reimburse the province when Treasury Board loosens the purse strings.
Each day of delay means that we will be that much longer escaping the grips of the overseas oil interests, pouring more dollars into already overloaded foreign coffers, denying Nova Scotians promised jobs, and depriving ourselves of the benefits of being able to use our own resources.
This frustration with the lack of movement on the development of the mine at Donkin is strongly felt. If it were started now, by 1985 it could replace through its two million tonne capacity in its first stage eight million barrels of oil at a price which, by 1985, could well be up to the spot market prices of today. This is an enormous opportunity for the coal industry.
Again I have here an article which appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald which has not been notable in the past for emphasizing this, but they saw the terrible foot-dragging by the previous government which carried on the feasibility study since last March 8, a study which is now being continued by this new government, while funds are not being allocated. That was the point I was trying to make to the Prime Minister.
It is all right to have an energy bank if it is for the purposes of funding, but right now we need $25 million to $30 million in order to start the tunnels in that mine, while the province is giving money to the Crown corporation to do the clearing and so on. We cannot wait another year, and it will take that long for the energy bank to get going.
Out of this frustration, again the Chronicle-Herald wrote a lead editorial on its front page. As the minister knows very well, it is not notably an NDP paper. On November 10, just the day before Remembrance Day, the following appeared:
The chief focus of this political indecision on energy matters is currently the proposal to develop the undersea Donkin mine in the vast Sydney coalfield, which contains 95 per cent of Nova Scotia's recoverable coal reserves. The economics of the mine proposal have been studied exhaustively by both levels of government, to the extent that the previous provincial government, convinced the mine was economic and would be in production by 1985, constructed a coal-fired generator at Lingan. The present provincial government, equally confident of the feasibility of Donkin, is continuing with a second Lingan unit and has begun clearing the site for the mine, hoping the federal Treasury Board will release the $220 million initial capital requirement before spring, when tunnelling is scheduled to begin.
... If Ottawa moves immediately, the mine can be producing by 1985

If we are to go to the world oil price or the Chicago price quickly, then that type of funding and bank could be important to the Atlantic region for the two reasons I have mentioned already: bringing the power from Newfoundland into a maritime power grid, and the development of the tidal power situation in Nova Scotia and on the perimeter of New Brunswick.
The first stage at Donkin, the tunnelling and so on, must be announced now. Otherwise, we will be into another year with more imported oil and the obscenely high unemployment will continue in Cape Breton. The province of Nova Scotia is agreed, generally everybody is agreed that we must move fast in order to build the tunnels and get into the production of coal. I do not think putting it off through an energy bank for another year will do anything to help the situation. In fact it will not only create frustrations within the area there, but also great frustrations in the provincial government in Halifax, which is a Tory government. Already they have put funds through the federal Crown agency to start the site with the hope and I imagine the promise they will be given back when Treasury Board loosens things.
The minister told me that this will be going before cabinet in two or three weeks. I say to the minister: do everything in your power to make sure the moneys are allocated, the $25 million to $30 million, now. If the minister is sincere in saying that he wants sufficiency in energy and that he wants to stop oil from coming into the country, then the answer for Nova Scotia, as its government has spelled out, must be in terms of greater coal development. The key is the earliest start possible for the Donkin mine. There is no disagreement between myself and the people I talk with in the provincial government at Halifax and the officials of the energy department in Halifax.
There is no disagreement between the people 1 have known here since 1960 when I was at the University of St. Francis Xavier. I would come up here and talk with them about coal when decisions were being made by the Diefenbaker govern-

ment as to whether they would close one, two, or three mines. They tell me, "You watch it now and make sure that the Donkin mine will not be shelved for anything else, because there are people who are trying to shelve it". If we have to wait for an energy bank down the road in a year, in order to get the funds, then all hell will break loose on this issue. Enough concern has been generated now.
The people of Cape Breton have been through enough frustration on this issue. Surely we can get action on this and start getting some of the unemployed people off the streets, as well as contribute to the greater good of Canada by displacing that very, very expensive imported oil, which will be much more expensive by the time the mine is finished.
1 see my time is just about up, but I should like to ask the minister to comment on the question of InterVac, a high technology industry operating out of Sydney. subtopic: NATIONAL UNITY-GOVERNMENT POLICY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION WITH QUEBEC
NATIONAL UNITY-GOVERNMENT POLICY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION WITH QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 31, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) whether his party had taken any position on the sovereignty-association proposal of the Parti Quebecois government and whether it was true that the Conservatives would be campaigning on both sides of the question during the Quebec referendum. I asked this question because on October 29 the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. La Salle) said in Montreal, as reported by the Montreal Gazette on October 30, as follows:
'The Progressive Conservative party should stay outside the (pro-federalist) umbrella committee because we have different objectives', Roch La Salle said yesterday.
'Our position is not the same as Mr. Ryan's,'-
The following day another Conservative minister from Quebec, Senator Asselin, was quoted in La Presse dated October 31, as follows:

It will not come under the "no" umbrella in the referendum campaign no matter what its leader. Prime Minister Joe Clark, says.
[Mr. Baker (Nepean-Carleton).J

When I put this question to the Prime Minister, the Minister of Supply and Services confirmed the news story by interjecting from his seat as follows:
Ask me the question and I will answer yes or no.
In other words, the Minister of Supply and Services wanted the House to know that he was ready to vote "Yes" or "No" on the referendum question, depending on what it was.
The Prime Minister never answered my question. He merely said, as he says so often, that the Conservative party, "is determined to work toward the strengthening of the federal system". That is a brave generality. By this he explained that he meant a new attitude toward the division of powers. He gave as examples the dismantling of Loto Canada and the granting of offshore mineral rights to Newfoundland and British Columbia. He went on to say, as reported at page 804 of Hansard:
It is my expectation that the question-
That is, the referendum question.
-will be phrased in such a way that members of the Progressive Conservative Party will want to vote against that question. That is my expectation of what will happen-but I have not seen the question proposed by Mr. Levesque: perhaps the hon. member has.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, he left the situation just as vague. He did not say clearly that the Conservative party would campaign for the "No" option and that they would participate with the umbrella committee campaigning against the "No" option on the referendum.
At that point in time the Parti Quebecois had not published their white paper on the referendum. Mr. Speaker, how could anyone be so naive as to think that a pro separatist government would put a referendum question to which a "Yes" answer would not favour their cause? How could the Prime Minister think for one minute that he or his ministers could vote "yes" in the referendum and still favour federalism? What kind of bluff was he trying to foist on the Canadian people?
1 suggest, Mr. Speaker, he was trying to walk on both sides of the fence, trying to assure anglo-Canadians outside Quebec that he stood for a united Canada, and trying to win, on the other hand, a bigger following in Quebec by courting the pro nationalist element in that province.
On November 1, Mr. Speaker, the Quebec government published its white paper on sovereignty-association and the referendum, and made its proposals more specific. Of course, it only became more clear that the Parti Quebecois wanted to break up the country before seeking an association which, I might say, would be weaker than the common market.
I quote from a summary of the white paper on page 13 as follows:
The only laws applying on Quebec's territory will be those adopted by the National Assembly, and the only taxes levied will be those decreed by Quebec law.
As a result of the publication of the white paper, Mr. Speaker, I asked the Prime Minister once again some similar questions on November 5. This time the Prime Minister said
November 12, 1979

that members of the Conservative party would participate in the umbrella committee supporting the federal system in the referendum, and that that was the intention of his two Quebec ministers as he "made it clear in the House the other day." I do not know what day he was talking about, Mr. Speaker. I reread all his answers in Hansard, particularly his answers on November 2. 1 can find no statement which makes clear that its Quebec ministers will campaign for the "no" option in the referendum. As a result, it is still unclear with respect to the Quebec ministers.
As reported at page 884, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Lalonde), the Prime Minister said:
The question is whether it would help the cause of federalism to have a federal minister from Quebec join a somewhat limited group formed by Mr. Ryan. I think that now that we are in a position to discuss party strategies here, it would probably be better for us to let the supporters join that umbrella committee and to let the federal ministers from Quebec or elsewhere show through their actions and their activities this government's determination to bring about a truly renewed federalism.
Once again he is waffling. He is saying that he prefers that the ministers do not participate. We still want some clear answers. Will he and his ministers participate in the referendum umbrella committee? Will he commit federal resources to rebutting the white paper from a Canadian point of view? Is he going to stand up for Canada, or is he going to leave this to the premiers, and is he going to continue to appease the pro-nationalist forces in Quebec?

subtopic: NATIONAL UNITY-GOVERNMENT POLICY ON SOVEREIGNTY-ASSOCIATION WITH QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be given this opportunity to respond to the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) on behalf of the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark).
The position of the government concerning the up-coming referendum in Quebec is clear. First, the government has stated that the proposal put forward by the Quebec government in its White Paper, the so-called sovereignty-association thesis, is incompatible with the federal system and totally unacceptable to this government. I fail to see how this position could be made more clear. Second, the Prime Minister has
Adjournment Debate
made it perfectly clear, in a reply to the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, that the Prime Minister, his ministers and members of the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, would work toward a victory of federal forces in the province of Quebec. Third, the Prime Minister has explained that our approach would be different from that of the previous administration.
The government in no way questions the sincerity of members of the opposite bench. But recent history has shown that much of their strategy was wrong and counter-productive. We do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that Quebeckers will be convinced of the merits of federalism by publicity campaigns, propaganda, or rhetoric, but rather by concrete acts of flexibility.
I sympathize with the hon. member. I respect his anxiety because it demonstrates his love for his country. But the hon. member, 1 would hope, would have more confidence in the good sense of Quebeckers. The great achievements of Quebec society during the last 20 years show that its people can move toward fulfilling their aspirations within federalism. On the day of the referendum I am confident that sc tenir debout to paraphrase Felix Leclerc, will mean Quebeckers will choose Canada.
Finally, I would like to say that all members in this House being dedicated federalists, it would be deplorable for us to be divided on this crucial issue. Federalist forces in Quebec will be rallying behind Mr. Ryan's leadership because that leadership is enshrined in law. In this chamber we may legitimately disagree in terms of day to day strategy. But I ask colleagues not to challenge the clarity or the dedication of this government's policy regarding the referendum.

subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT-AGREEMENT WITH U.S. ON REDUCTION OF AIR POLLUTANTS
THE ENVIRONMENT-AGREEMENT WITH U.S. ON REDUCTION OF AIR POLLUTANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, acid rain has been described by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Fraser) as the most serious threat to our environment today. Yet his policy to combat it, at home and abroad, is hesitant, weak, and at times contradictory. On the one hand he is quoted as saying, "Our appeals for more U.S. controls will likely fall on deaf ears if we do not begin to clean up our own act". On the other hand he says we must wait for an agreement with the U.S. before we take any action at home, because it would not do any good to reduce emissions in Ontario without cleaning up U.S. industries.
When the minister appeared before the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry last week, buried on page 8 he had a one paragraph statement to the effect that acid precipitation is one area which requires priority attention. Beyond that, we do not know what his plan of action is. For instance, what are the steps he plans to take to establish federal-provincial co-operation? All we hear is that there is a problem and that something should be done, sometime. He talks of taking action, and then

November 12, 1979
Adjournment Debate
all he does is outline efforts to strengthen monitoring and research, efforts initiated by the previous government. It looks more and more that what he means by giving priority attention to an issue and taking action is that he intends to redefine the problem while at the same time remaining vague as to how and when solutions will be reached.
Last July the minister was reported to have said that Canada is "very close" to signing a diplomatic agreement with the United States that will set the stage for a full scale treaty to cut down acid rain and other forms of international air pollution. He said, "We are so very close and I want the- initial-agreement very much . . . The time to sign this treaty is right now." Soon after, though, he began to say that we should not expect an agreement before the U.S. presidential elections in 1980, that this was a realistic date and that it would be irresponsible to raise expectations. When I asked him to tell us the source of the information concerning the date after the presidential election, he told us at the standing committee meeting of November 8 that it was an assumption, and that the information was not based on consultation with Washington. Why, then, on the basis of such assumptions, should we accept a date of some time in 1981?
Why can we not wait? First, because the destructive and cumulative damage to the environment increases slowly but inexorably with every day, week, and month that go by. What do we need to see happen to get this government moving?
Second, because we may well be making a wrong assessment of President Carter's priorities. Why are we concluding that he cannot sign a treaty in an election year, considering his record on environmental matters?
Third, because apparently the United States has higher emission control standards than Canada. With this in mind, it would seem that we have a lot of catching up to do right here before we can start to move with the United States, "equally" as the minister puts it.
Add to the minister's hesitancy and contradictions the provinces' reluctance to confront industry. In the case of Inco, the largest single source of acid precipitation in North America, it was ordered by the Ontario government some years ago to cut sulphur dioxide emissions to 750 tons a day by December 31, 1978. Yet Inco we learn has been allowed to emit 3,600 tons a day until June 30, 1982. Mr. Parrott was reported last week to have said that acid rain could be prevented, but that the cost is too high and there is a complicated problem of what to do with that material once removed from the atmosphere. This implies in the mind of the provincial government of Ontario that we have at the present time little hope except to let precipitation do irreparable damage to our environment. What a shame, Mr. Speaker! If you think that is bad, listen to this.
The federal Minister of the Environment is quoted as saying that to push Canadian industry to the same standards as the U.S., or beyond, would harm, imagine, our competitive position. He said, "You cannot go to Canadian industry and say you have to meet certain requirements" just to show Canada is serious about fighting acid rain. Why not? Are we not serious? How can the most serious threat to our environment, which is

largely caused by industry, be resolved without affecting certain interests, be they of an industry, of consumers, or of society at large. Is this being realistic?
On the other hand the minister is quoted as saying that, "Although substantial resistance might be expected in Canada from those affected by such costs, I would point out, in such countries as the United States and Japan, up to 20 per cent of the capital cost of new facilities is not being expanded on pollution control". This was in an interview over CJOH on September 25. It goes to prove that a country can be competitive, as Japan is, as well as being environmentally responsible.
To sum up, we in the opposition are asking the government to stop dilly-dallying and to give this matter top priority. We are asking the Government of Canada, (1) to press Washington for an early date in 1980, as the time when we want to sign an international agreement in the interest of both countries and (2), to pressure the provinces incessantly and without delay so as to get them to act within the scope of their responsibility and, if they are reluctant, as is the case in Ontario, to invoke the powers given to the federal government under our constitution to proceed unilaterally.
The environment is in grave danger. Therefore, in the long run we are in grave danger too. We do not want to reach the state of an emergency just because of federal-provincial minuets. Air does not know provincial boundaries, neither does water. We cannot let procedural and political delays destroy our environment. What is at stake today is a healthy environment and tomorrow the health, and maybe the survival, of the human species.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Postmaster General and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT-AGREEMENT WITH U.S. ON REDUCTION OF AIR POLLUTANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister indicated in his response to the hon. member, and he reiterated his position in the standing committee having to do with the estimates of that department, that he would welcome, as he emphatically stated in this House, the signing of an effective Canada-United States agreement having to do with the abatement of this very serious problem.
The judgment that such an agreement cannot be reached until 1980 or after the U.S. elections is his own. In coming to this conclusion the minister has taken into consideration the results of the meeting he held on August 8 with his counterpart in Washington and the advice of his own departmental officials in consultation with those of the Department of External Affairs. May 1 emphasize, in addition, that the problem we now face, and which has been described as so serious a matter, is not one which simply arose since May 22, and the minister takes the position that he must be realistic despite the seriousness of the matter and despite the priority which his department gives to it.
It would not be responsible for him to give the kinds of assurances which are being requested by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), and he does not wish to raise such unrealistic expectations in the mind of the public. It is his view
November 12, 1979

that while this is not a new problem, as 1 mentioned earlier, its solution will take time. I suggest it will take time to identify the sources of the emissions, the technology of the control which will be required for each, to identify the aspects of law which will have to be applied both on this and on the American side of the river, and then to negotiate an international agreement acceptable to both governments. This process cannot take place tomorrow.
The minister has instructed his officials to ensure that in co-operation with the provinces they undertake all the necessary preparatory work so that an agreement can be signed as soon as a U.S. election is over or a United States President is prepared to enter into such an agreement.
If I might refer specifically to the concerns of Canada and the reduction of Canadian emissions in acid-causing pollution, a federal-provincial committee on control strategy has already begun to identify, develop, and evaluate alternative abatement policies. This initial work will be completed in the spring, and this government's intention is to rely on the provinces to put in place the needed control.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-NEW BRUNSWICK-INQUIRY WHETHER MINISTER WILL CONDUCT INVESTIGATION INTO SUSPENSION OF CERTAIN BENEFITS
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-NEW BRUNSWICK-INQUIRY WHETHER MINISTER WILL CONDUCT INVESTIGATION INTO SUSPENSION OF CERTAIN BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, November 2, I rose under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to ask for an urgent inquiry into the problem of seasonal farm workers who have become unemployed in the economic region of Madawaska, an area that actually includes the three provincial counties of Madawaska, Victoria and Carleton in northwestern New Brunswick.
The purpose of my motion was to ask the minister to inquire and send on the spot one or several officials to report to him in the shortest possible time. Prior to my motion in the House of Commons, I sent the minister an urgent letter on Monday, October 29, in which 1 related to him the demonstrations and the climate of tension surrounding those incidents among both benefit recipients and government officials. I still have not received an answer to that letter and I do not accept the answers given later on in the House by the minister as satisfactory.
Still on Friday, November 2, I came back during question period to ask the minister when he intended to study the demands of seasonal workers being deprived of benefits for which several of them believed they had worked during the whole spring period planting trees for forest companies in New
Adjournment Debate
Brunswick, this summer on broccoli crops for processors again in New Brunswick, and others on cucumber, tomato and tobacco crops in southern Ontario. The minister replied that he was directing attention to the situation.
He stated that it was difficult to evaluate the situation and admitted in his reply that there were examples of unfairness in the application of amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. In the same breath, the minister agreed to examine the situation to see if he could provide some relief. In answer to a supplementary 1 put to him, the minister finally stated that the long-term solution to this particular problem was to find employment for the people receiving unemployment insurance. 1 certainly admire the minister's intentions and I will gladly support any sincere and serious attempt on his part to do so.
Last November 5 I met with a group of unemployed and their spokesman to explain the legislation to them and the recourse and appeal procedures it provides. 1 had many discussions with the employment centre director and the local Unemployment Insurance Commission staff. They are all awaiting some directive from above, from the minister or one of his senior officials, but the reply has yet to come and the situation has far from improved. Demonstrations continue and are becoming agitated or noisy to the extent that the police can hardly contain them.
The minister is not only responsible for the sound administration of the unemployment insurance system, he is also under the obligation of introducing in the House all amendments or changes which would make the system fairer, more humane and easier to apply. I urge him to act quickly in this respect. He can be assured of my support if he does so, just as I have always reacted vociferously against all the exaggerated and sometimes illogical proposals put forth by his predecessors.
I have been a member of Parliament for nearly 12 years and 1 can assure him immediately that 1 shall co-operate fully to humanize the present system. I am not at all interested in making petty politics on the backs of the workers. What makes me sad and sometimes angry is to hear certain members or other residents of economically strong areas like southern Ontario suggest that the people of the Atlantic region are lazy and do not want to work and that we should cut them off from all unemployment insurance benefits to force them back to work. We still hear this from the rich areas of the country.
Would the minister try to suggest that the 250-odd families from Madawaska and Victoria who went-men, women and children-to pick vegetables in southern Ontario, are lazy? Was it laziness on their part to work 10, 12, 13 hours or more each day from early July until October in Ontario fields, even though very often this meant that their children missed school? Does he think that those people went to southern Ontario to spend their holidays and that they would have gone if there had been work available in New Brunswick? Come on! It is time to act, and one of the things that could be done

November 12, 1979
Adjournment Debate
would be to remove from the Madawaska economic area Carleton county which is now causing a serious distortion of the employment situation and unemployment levels in Mada-waska-Victoria. Seasonal workers were not able to get as many weeks of work this year as last year, and because of this they have been excluded from benefits through no fault of theirs. Winter is coming. In fact, it is already quite cold in my area of New Brunswick and we must do something to help the workers and the families of workers who are entitled to unemployment insurance benefits. We should do so also if we want good workers from Madawaska and Victoria for the harvest in Ontario next summer. Something must be done immediately to rectify the inequities of the present system.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-NEW BRUNSWICK-INQUIRY WHETHER MINISTER WILL CONDUCT INVESTIGATION INTO SUSPENSION OF CERTAIN BENEFITS

I would like to add that the ministry is very well aware of the fact that changes in legislation and regulations can sometimes cause problems to some individuals. We are equally aware that the repeater regulation, in increasing the number of weeks required to qualify for benefits, has resulted in a situation where some who would previously have been eligible for benefits do not now qualify.
Any time that such a policy change may be detrimental to individuals, naturally we are concerned. In this case we are concerned with any potential negative effects it may have and we hope they will be minimized.
As the minister said, the best way to reduce these negative effects is to increase the employment opportunities for the unemployed. To this end, the minister has already taken action to extend the deadline for the receipt of Canada Works applications. This step will improve access to funds available for job creation purposes.
In so doing we are able to facilitate the creation of an increased number of employment opportunities which will contribute positively to the local economy. This alternative also provides the opportunity to create jobs, not only for those who are affected in this particular instance, but also for other unemployed workers in the Edmundston area. 1 am convinced that these changes as proposed by the ministry will deal positively and effectively with the current situation.
